name: graphicx
desc: Adds `\includegraphics` for placing PNG, PDF and JPEG images, with keys to scale, rotate and crop them. With XeLaTeX, SVG files cannot be included directly. Convert them to PDF or PNG first.
details:
`graphicx` is the workhorse for images. It redefines `\includegraphics` with a key–value interface, so you can scale (`width=0.5\textwidth`), rotate (`angle=90`), crop (`trim=...`, `clip`), and pick a page from a multi-page PDF (`page=2`). Prefer relative widths like `width=\linewidth` over absolute centimetres so the figure adapts to the page layout.

Under pdfLaTeX the package natively handles PDF, PNG, and JPEG; EPS must be converted (see `epstopdf`). Under XeLaTeX it handles PDF/PNG/JPEG but **not** SVG — convert SVG to PDF or PNG first. Organise images with `\graphicspath{{figures/}}` so you can write `\includegraphics{plot}` without a path.

Images normally live inside a `figure` float with `\caption` and `\label`, so they can be cross-referenced with `\ref` or `\cref`. A frequent pitfall is forgetting `\centering` inside the float — `\includegraphics` alone does not centre the image. Another is embedding huge raster images; downscale them beforehand to keep the PDF small.

name: amsmath
desc:
Provides aligned multi-line equations, matrices, cases and many extra math operators. Use it in any document with more than trivial formulas.

Do not use `eqnarray`, because `align` spaces correctly. Load `amsmath` before `hyperref`.
details:
`amsmath` is the foundation of serious mathematical typesetting in LaTeX. It provides the `align`/`gather`/`multline` environments for multi-line equations, `cases` for piecewise definitions, `pmatrix`/`bmatrix`/`vmatrix` matrix environments, `\operatorname` for custom operators, `\text{}` inside maths, and dozens of refinements to spacing, `\frac`, and `\sum`. Almost every maths-heavy document loads it, usually immediately after the document class.

A big reason it exists is that the built-in `eqnarray` environment spaces relations badly (it treats `=` as a normal symbol). Use `align` instead: `\begin{align} a &= b + c \\ d &= e \end{align}`. The `&` marks the alignment point and `\\` ends a row. Load `amsmath` **before** `hyperref`; loading it afterwards can break `\eqref` and cause subtle problems.

`amsmath` is so fundamental that several packages build directly on it — `amssymb`, `amsthm`, `mathtools`, and `bm` all expect it to be loaded first. If you find yourself wanting a patch (a missing delimiter size, a bug in `\smash`), reach for `mathtools`, which loads `amsmath` and fixes its shortcomings.

name: amssymb
desc: Adds hundreds of additional symbols (e.g., blackboard bold, script letters, special arrows) that are missing from basic LaTeX. Load it after `amsmath`.
details:
`amssymb` loads the two AMS symbol fonts (`msam` and `msbm`) and exposes their glyphs as commands. That is how you get `\mathbb{R}` (blackboard bold), `\mathfrak{g}` (Fraktur), `\varnothing`, `\therefore`, `\lesssim`, `\nmid`, and many arrows and operators that plain LaTeX lacks. It also makes `\mathbb` available, which is why so many documents write `\mathbb{R}`, `\mathbb{N}`, `\mathbb{C}` for number sets.

`amssymb` internally loads `amsfonts`, so you rarely need to load `amsfonts` yourself. It should come after `amsmath` in the preamble. Because it is font-based, the symbols are only available in pdfLaTeX's traditional font setup; with XeLaTeX/LuaLaTeX and `unicode-math`, most of these commands still work but are mapped to Unicode codepoints via the math font.

If you only need a couple of symbols, you can still load `amssymb` — it is small and harmless. One subtlety: `\mathbb` produces blackboard bold only for uppercase letters; for lowercase or digits use `bbm` or `dsfont`.

name: amsthm
desc: Provides ready‑made environments for theorems, lemmas, definitions, proofs, etc., following the style of American Mathematical Society publications. Load it after `amsmath`.
details:
`amsthm` supplies the semantic environments every maths paper needs: `theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, `definition`, `remark`, `example`, and `proof` (which ends with a ∎). It also gives you `
ewtheorem` for defining your own numbered environments and `
ewtheorem*` for unnumbered ones. The `proof` environment automatically inserts an italic *Proof.* and a QED symbol.

A typical setup is: `
ewtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[section]` (number theorems within sections), then `
ewtheorem{lemma}[theorem]{Lemma}` (share the theorem counter so a lemma and theorem are numbered in one sequence). The optional `[section]` ties numbering to section counters, which keeps references readable.

`amsthm` also provides `	heoremstyle{plain|definition|remark}` to change the visual style of environments. It must be loaded after `amsmath`, and it plays nicely with `mathtools` and `hyperref`. If you need per-chapter numbering in a book, use `
ewtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[chapter]` and remember to reset counters appropriately.

name: mathtools
desc: Fixes several shortcomings of `amsmath` and adds useful tools such as `\coloneqq`, `\DeclarePairedDelimiter`, and `\mathclap`. Load it instead of `amsmath` to get both.
details:
`mathtools` is best thought of as "`amsmath` done right". It loads `amsmath` and patches several of its known issues, then adds a toolbox of its own. The most popular feature is `\DeclarePairedDelimiter{\abs}{\lvert}{\rvert}`, which creates an `\abs{x}` command whose size adapts — `\abs*{x}` auto-sizes, `\abs[\big]{x}` forces a size, and `\abs{x}` uses the natural size.

Other highlights: `\coloneqq` and `\eqqcolon` for properly spaced definition symbols; `\mathclap`/`\mathllap`/`\mathrlap` for overlapping content in subscripts (very useful under `\sum` limits); `dcases` and `rcases` for display-style `cases`; `\shortintertext`; and the `pmatrix*` family that takes alignment options. There is also `\xleftrightarrow` and friends for extensible arrows.

The rule of thumb is simple: if you use `amsmath`, use `mathtools` instead — it is a strict superset. Load it **before** `hyperref` just like `amsmath`, and note that some packages (e.g. `empheq`) build on `mathtools`.

name: bm
desc: Provides a reliable way to make individual math symbols bold (e.g., `\bm{\alpha}`) with correct spacing and delimiter handling. Load it after `amsmath`.
details:
Bold mathematics is surprisingly subtle. `\mathbf{...}` only affects Latin letters and ignores Greek symbols; `\boldsymbol` (from `amsmath`) works but mishandles some spacing and delimiter cases. `bm` provides `\bm{...}`, which bolds **any** math symbol — Greek letters, operators, fractions, and whole sub-expressions — while preserving spacing and correctly handling large delimiters.

Typical usage: `\bm{\alpha}`, `\bm{x}`, `\bm{\nabla}`, and inside an expression `\bm{v} = \bm{\omega} \times \bm{r}`. Vectors and matrices written with `\bm` look consistent because the bolding respects the surrounding math axis.

Load `bm` after `amsmath`. One caveat: `bm` uses an internal trick that can clash with `unicode-math`; for XeLaTeX/LuaLaTeX, use `\symbf{...}` from `unicode-math` (which `bm` is not designed to replace). In pdfLaTeX, `bm` is the standard choice for bold vectors and tensors.

name: siunitx
desc: Typesets physical quantities, units, and numbers consistently (e.g., `\SI{9.81}{\metre\per\second\squared}`). It also aligns numbers in tables and follows international standards.
details:
`siunitx` solves the surprisingly hard problem of printing numbers and units correctly. It understands SI prefixes, derived units, uncertainties, and significant figures, and it follows the ISO 80000 conventions automatically (thin space between number and unit, correct superscripts for powers, proper degree and per signs). Use `\num{1234.5}`, `\unit{\metre\per\second\squared}`, or combine them with `\qty{9.81}{\metre\per\second\squared}` (the modern name; `\SI` is the older equivalent).

Beyond simple quantities, `siunitx` shines in tables: the `S` column type aligns numbers by their decimal point (and by uncertainty, if given). Set up your document once with `\sisetup{...}` — e.g. `group-digits=integer`, `per-mode=symbol`, `detect-all` — and every number in the document will follow the same conventions.

It replaces the older `units` and `SIunits` packages. It also offers `\ang{...}` for angles, `\complexnum`, `\numlist`, and `\qtylist`. Load it in the preamble; if you have a lot of `S` columns, include `\sisetup{table-number-alignment=center}`. Its only real drawback is that it is heavy and can slow large table-heavy documents, but for scientific writing it is essential.

name: geometry
desc: Lets you set page size, margins, orientation, and other layout parameters with a simple key–value interface (e.g., `\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}`).
details:
`geometry` gives you direct, readable control over the page geometry that LaTeX normally sets in a labyrinth of length parameters (`\textwidth`, `\oddsidemargin`, `\topmargin`, …). Instead you write `\usepackage[a4paper, margin=2.5cm]{geometry}` or specify `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`, `bindingoffset`, `headheight`, `includehead`, `includefoot`, `landscape`, and more.

For asymmetric layouts — e.g. a binding edge on a book — use `inner=`/`outer=` instead of `left=`/`right=`. For two-sided documents, `twoside` plus `bindingoffset` gives correct gutter margins on alternate pages. `geometry` also provides `\newgeometry{...}` and `\restoregeometry` so you can change layout mid-document (for a full-page figure, for example).

A common mistake is specifying both `left`/`right` and `hmargin` at once — `geometry` will complain. Another is forgetting that `geometry` sets `\textwidth` after `\usepackage`, so packages loaded later that depend on the text width (e.g. some table and `tikz` configurations) will see the new value. Load `geometry` early in the preamble to be safe.

name: hyperref
desc: Turns cross‑references, citations, and URLs into clickable links, adds PDF bookmarks, and sets PDF metadata (title, author). Load it last (or almost last) in the preamble.
details:
`hyperref` is the package that makes your PDF interactive: `\ref` and `\cite` become clickable, `\url` produces a live link, the table of contents becomes navigable bookmarks, and the PDF carries title, author, and keyword metadata. It does this by patching many core commands, so the golden rule is to load it **last** in the preamble (or almost last — just before packages that explicitly need to come after it, like `cleveref`).

Useful options include `colorlinks=true` (coloured text instead of ugly boxes), `linkcolor=blue`, `citecolor=green`, `urlcolor=blue`, `bookmarks=true`, `pdfauthor={...}`, and `pdftitle={...}`. If you want the classic boxed links, set `hidelinks` to remove them or `pdfborder={0 0 1}` to style them.

`hyperref` has a long history of clashing with other packages; the main workarounds are loading order, using `\usepackage{hyperref}` then `\usepackage{cleveref}` (which patches `hyperref`'s references), and preferring `\autoref`/`\cref` over `\ref` if you want names. In modern documents you may prefer `\usepackage[hidelinks]{hyperref}` plus `xcolor` for custom link colouring. Be aware that `hyperref` interacts with `amsmath` (`\eqref`) — load `amsmath` first.

name: cleveref
desc: Automatically inserts the correct word (e.g., “Theorem”, “Figure”, “Section”) before a reference number. Load it after `hyperref`.
details:
`cleveref` upgrades cross-referencing. Instead of writing "see Figure~\ref{fig:plot}" (and remembering the `~` for a non-breaking space), you write "see \cref{fig:plot}" and it prints "see Figure 3" — with the right noun for the target's type (figure, table, theorem, section, equation, …). Multiple references are sorted and grouped automatically: `\cref{a,b,c}` might produce "Figures 1–3".

The command family is `\cref` (lowercase noun), `\Cref` (capitalised), `\crefrange` (ranges), `\labelcref` (number only), and `\namecref` (name only). You configure the nouns once with `\crefname{figure}{figure}{figures}` and can tell `cleveref` about custom theorem environments via `\crefname` and `\Crefname` so it does not call them "theorems" when they are lemmas.

`cleveref` must be loaded **after** `hyperref` because it patches `hyperref`'s reference machinery. If you use `babel`, load `cleveref` after `babel` too. It does not work well with some very old packages, but in modern documents it is essentially standard. Pair it with `hyperref`'s `\autoref` only if you have a reason to — `cleveref` is more flexible.

name: xcolor
desc: Provides driver‑independent colour commands (e.g., `\textcolor{red}{text}`, `\colorbox{yellow}{text}`) and supports tints, shades, and mixing. It supersedes the older `color` package.
details:
`xcolor` is the standard colour package. It supersedes the older `color` package and adds named models (`rgb`, `RGB`, `HTML`, `cmyk`, `gray`, `hsb`), colour mixing, and a large set of pre-defined named colours like `red!50!blue` (50 % red mixed with blue). You can define your own with `\definecolor{myblue}{HTML}{1F77B4}` and then use `\textcolor{myblue}{text}`, `\colorbox{myblue}{...}`, or set a global `\color{myblue}`.

It also provides `\colorlet{alias}{...}` for creating variants, `\rowcolors` (via the `table` option) for alternating row colours in tables, and options like `table`, `dvipsnames`, `svgnames`, and `x11names` to load additional named colours. For tables, the `table` option enables `\rowcolors{2}{gray!10}{white}` — very useful for striped tables.

`xcolor` is a dependency of many packages (`tikz`, `hyperref`, `booktabs` is independent, but `tcolorbox` etc. depend on it). Load it early. If you need `\colorbox` with rounded corners or borders, that is `tcolorbox` or `mdframed` territory; `xcolor` only colours the background. A gotcha: `xcolor` with the `table` option redefines `\rowcolors`; if you also use `colortbl`, load order matters.

name: booktabs
desc: Adds commands like `\toprule`, `\midrule`, and `\bottomrule` to produce tables with clean, publication‑quality horizontal rules, avoiding vertical lines.
details:
`booktabs` implements the typographic advice of the book *Publication Quality Tables* — namely: use horizontal rules only, make them thin at the edges and slightly heavier in the middle, and never use vertical rules. It provides `\toprule`, `\midrule`, `\bottomrule`, plus `\cmidrule(lr){2-3}` for partial rules and `\addlinespace` for extra vertical breathing room between logical row groups.

A typical table looks like `\begin{tabular}{lrr} \toprule Model & RMSE & MAE \\ \midrule A & 0.12 & 0.09 \\ B & 0.15 & 0.11 \\ \bottomrule \end{tabular}`. The three-rule pattern (top/mid/bottom) is the hallmark of a clean table; use `\cmidrule` to group header columns and `\addlinespace` to separate logical blocks.

`booktabs` rules are deliberately not compatible with vertical rules (`|` in the column spec), because vertical lines fight with the rules' spacing. If you truly need vertical rules, you are fighting the package — prefer `tabularx` or `tabularray` for complex layouts. `booktabs` also pairs beautifully with `siunitx` (S columns) and `multirow`. It does not work inside `tabular` with `\\*` tricks — use `\addlinespace` for extra space instead.

name: multirow
desc: Allows a single table cell to span several rows (e.g., `\multirow{2}{*}{Text}`). Works well together with `booktabs` and `longtable`.
details:
`multirow` lets a cell occupy several rows, which is essential for grouped tables like a category label spanning three models. The syntax is `\multirow{nrows}{width}{text}`; use `*` for the width to let LaTeX size the column naturally: `\multirow{2}{*}{Group A}`. The vertical position of the text can be tuned with an optional argument: `\multirow{2}[1]{*}{Text}` or `\multirow{2}[-1]{*}{...}` to nudge it up or down.

It is most often used to replace repeated entries: instead of writing "Group A" on every row, put `\multirow{3}{*}{Group A}` in the first row and leave the next two cells empty (or use `\multirow{3}{*}{}` for the empty continuation). For the opposite (spanning columns), use `\multicolumn`, which is built into LaTeX itself.

`multirow` pairs well with `booktabs`: the vertical nudge argument is often needed because `booktabs` rules add height. It also works inside `longtable`. A common mistake is forgetting to leave the subsequent cells empty; `multirow` does not suppress rules or borders by itself, and overlapping text is a sign you used the wrong number of rows.

name: longtable
desc: Enables tables longer than one page, with repeated headers and captions. It is more flexible than the older `supertabular`.
details:
`longtable` is for tables that cannot fit on a single page. Unlike `tabular`, which is a single box, a `longtable` can break at row boundaries across page breaks, optionally repeating its header and footer. The environment supports `\endfirsthead`, `\endhead`, `\endfoot`, and `\endlastfoot` so you can define different content for the first page, all pages, and the last page.

A minimal pattern: `\begin{longtable}{ll} \toprule A & B \\ \midrule \endfirsthead \toprule A & B \\ \midrule \endhead \bottomrule \endfoot ... rows ... \end{longtable}`. The header block is repeated on every page automatically; you do not need to re-declare it manually.

`longtable` is finicky about floats: it cannot be placed inside a `table` float, and it cannot use `\caption` in the usual way — use `\caption{...} \\` inside the table body (usually before the first `\endfirsthead`). It works with `booktabs`, `multirow`, and `siunitx`'s `S` columns, though `S` columns need care. If you want a table that is *both* long and has automatic column widths, consider `xltabular` (a wrapper combining `tabularx` and `longtable`).

name: tabularx
desc: Defines an `X` column type that expands to fill the available width, making it easy to create tables that adapt to the page width.
details:
`tabularx` solves the "my table is too wide / too narrow" problem. You give the environment a total width — usually `\textwidth` — and use `X` columns, which automatically share whatever space is left after the fixed-width columns are placed. Syntax: `\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{lX} Name & Description that wraps automatically \end{tabularx}`.

You can customise the alignment of `X` columns with `>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X` (for ragged-right text), `>{\centering\arraybackslash}X`, or `>{\hsize=...}X`. The `\arraybackslash` is important — it restores `\\` inside the column so rows terminate correctly. The package also offers `\newcolumntype` (from `array`) to define reusable variants.

`tabularx` cannot break across pages; for that, use `longtable` or `xltabular` (which combines both). It also cannot be nested inside a `tabular` easily. The `X` column is often the right answer for specification tables, comparison tables, and any table with a long prose column. Pair it with `booktabs` for the rules and `siunitx` for numeric columns (though mixing `S` and `X` requires care).

name: array
desc: Extends the standard `array` and `tabular` environments with additional column formatting options (e.g., `>{...}`, `<{...}`) and programmable column specifications.
details:
The `array` package extends LaTeX's table machinery in two important ways. First, it adds the `>{...}` and `<{...}` column modifiers, which inject code at the start or end of every cell in a column — e.g. `>{$}c<{$}` makes a column maths-mode automatically, and `>{\bfseries}l` makes a column bold. Second, it provides `\newcolumntype`, letting you define reusable column types like `\newcolumntype{C}{>{\centering\arraybackslash}X}`.

The package also improves the `array` environment (the math-mode equivalent of `tabular`), handles `\multicolumn` more robustly, and provides better vertical alignment. The `m{...}` column type (vertically centred) is reworked, and `\extrarowheight` lets you add a little height to every row for a more open look — very useful when cells contain `\rule` or subscripts.

`array` is almost always loaded implicitly by `tabularx` and `booktabs`-adjacent workflows, but you should load it explicitly if you use `>{...}` or `\newcolumntype`. Its main gotcha is that `>{...}` content runs before the cell, so you must end it with `\arraybackslash` if you want to redefine `\\` — otherwise `\centering` inside a column breaks row endings. It is compatible with `booktabs`, `multirow`, and `siunitx`.

name: makecell
desc: Provides commands for multi‑line cells (`\makecell`), extra vertical space around cells, and consistent formatting of column heads.
details:
`makecell` fills a gap that `multirow` and `tabularx` leave: it gives you an easy way to put multi-line content inside a single cell. `\makecell{Line 1 \\ Line 2}` creates a cell with line breaks, and it works inside `tabular`, `tabularx`, and even inside `\multirow`. There is also `\thead{...}` for a centred, bold column header that can itself wrap, and `\makecell[...]` to control the vertical alignment.

A very useful feature is `\setcellgapes{...}` and `\makegapedcells`, which add a consistent amount of vertical padding to every cell in the following table — a much cleaner alternative to sprinkling `\rule` or `\addlinespace` everywhere. `\Xhline{...}` lets you draw a rule of a chosen thickness.

The package is small and works well with `booktabs`: combining `\thead` with `\toprule`/`\midrule` gives a clean header, and `\makecell` lets you break long header text without resorting to `p{}` columns. It also handles the sometimes-awkward combination of `\multirow` and multi-line cells. If you need even more control, consider `tabularray` or `nicematrix`, but `makecell` covers 90 % of everyday needs.

name: rotating
desc: Offers environments such as `sidewaysfigure` and `sidewaystable` to rotate floats and their captions by 90 degrees.
details:
`rotating` provides the `sidewaysfigure` and `sidewaystable` floats, which rotate their contents 90 degrees so that wide figures and tables fit on a portrait page. The caption rotates with the content (unlike manually rotating just the graphic with `\rotatebox`), and the float still participates in the normal float queues, so it moves to the top or bottom of a page like any `figure`.

There is also a `rotate` environment (non-floating) and the commands `\rotcaption` and `\turnbox`. The `sidewaysfigure`/`sidewaystable` approach is the standard way to include a wide table (e.g. many columns of results) while keeping the caption readable when the page is turned.

For PDF output, the rotated page itself is **not** rotated — only the content box is. This is usually what you want, but if you need the whole page to be landscape (viewers rotate it automatically), use `pdflscape` instead. `rotating` works with `hyperref`; however, the rotated caption and the `\label` must be handled carefully — `\caption` inside a `sidewaysfigure` rotates correctly with recent versions of `hyperref`. If you need landscape *pages* rather than rotated floats, combine with `lscape` or `pdflscape`.

name: pdflscape
desc: Adds PDF `/Rotate` support to the `lscape` package so that landscape pages are displayed correctly by PDF viewers.
details:
`pdflscape` is a thin wrapper around `lscape` that adds the crucial missing piece: it emits the PDF `/Rotate` page attribute. The base `lscape` package rotates the *content* of a page by 90 degrees but leaves the page in portrait orientation, so PDF viewers show the page sideways and the reader has to rotate their head or their PDF viewer. `pdflscape` makes the page itself landscape so viewers display it upright.

Usage is simple: `\begin{landscape} ... \end{landscape}`. Everything inside is typeset in landscape orientation, and the PDF page is marked as rotated. The content is usually a wide table or a large figure that does not fit in portrait.

It has no effect on DVI output (where rotation is not applicable), but for pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX, and LuaLaTeX it does exactly what you want. Note that floats inside a `landscape` environment still float within that environment — combine it with `table`/`figure` floats as usual, and use `rotating`'s `sidewaystable` only if you want a single rotated float rather than a whole landscape page.

name: setspace
desc: Provides easy control of line spacing (single, one‑and‑a‑half, double) via options or commands such as `\onehalfspacing`.
details:
`setspace` gives you predictable control over line spacing without disturbing the spacing that LaTeX applies around floats, footnotes, and maths. The main commands are `\singlespacing`, `\onehalfspacing`, and `\doublespacing`, plus the `spacing` environment (`\begin{spacing}{1.5} ... \end{spacing}`) for local changes and `\setstretch{1.25}` for a custom factor.

The key advantage over the naive `\renewcommand{\baselinestretch}{1.5}` is that `setspace` adjusts the stretch **at the right places** — footnotes and floats stay single-spaced by default, and it cooperates correctly with lists and display maths. The `doublespacing` command also takes care of the `\baselineskip` for figure and table captions.

The `setspace` package is often used in theses and journal submissions where double spacing is required. If your document class already sets spacing (e.g. `article`'s options), `setspace` still works but you should check the resulting line height against your institution's guidelines. Load it in the preamble; it is lightweight and has no significant conflicts.

name: fancyhdr
desc: Gives extensive control over page headers and footers, including different left/right pages and rules. It is the standard package for this task.
details:
`fancyhdr` is the standard way to customise running headers and footers. You call `\pagestyle{fancy}` and then set `\fancyhead[L]{...}`, `\fancyhead[R]{...}`, `\fancyfoot[C]{\thepage}`, etc. The bracket argument specifies position: `L`/`C`/`R` for odd pages, `LE`/`CE`/`RE` or `LO`/`CO`/`RO` for even/odd pages in two-sided documents, and `E`/`O` as shorthand for even/odd.

You can also use `\fancyhead[RO,LE]{...}` to put the same content in the right position on odd pages and the left on even pages (the classic book pattern). The package provides `\leftmark` and `\rightmark` for chapter/section names, `\headrulewidth` and `\footrulewidth` to control the rule lines, and `\fancyhf{}` to clear everything before building up a custom layout.

A common pitfall: in `book`/`report` classes, `\chapter` issues `\thispagestyle{plain}` on chapter-opening pages, so your fancy header disappears there — you may need `\fancypagestyle{plain}{...}` to redefine it. Also, `fancyhdr` requires the header height to be large enough for the content; if you get warnings about `\headheight`, set `\setlength{\headheight}{...}` or use `geometry`'s `headheight` option.

name: titlesec
desc: Allows you to change the format, font, spacing, and layout of chapter, section, and subsection titles.
details:
`titlesec` gives you precise control over the appearance of sectioning commands. The main command is `\titleformat{\section}{format}{label}{sep}{before-code}[after-code]`, where you specify the font (e.g. `\Large\bfseries`), the label (`\thesection`), the separation, and optional code before and after the title. `\titlespacing{command}{left}{before}{after}` controls the surrounding whitespace.

For example, `\titleformat{\section}{\normalfont\Large\bfseries}{\thesection}{1em}{}` makes sections bold and large with a normal-spaced number; adding `[\vspace{0.5ex}]` after the title adds space beneath. The package also provides `\titleformat*` (short form), `\titlespacing*`, and `\titleline` for a horizontal rule next to the title.

It works with `book`/`report`/`article`, but in `book`-like classes you also need `\titleformat{\chapter}[display]{...}{...}{...}{...}` for chapters. `titlesec` can clash with `hyperref` if the title format removes the anchor — for clickable section titles, use `\usepackage[explicit]{titlesec}` and `\texorpdfstring`. It also has an option `compact` to reduce spacing. If you use `memoir` or KOMA-Script classes, their built-in mechanisms are usually preferred over `titlesec`.

name: enumitem
desc: Provides fine‑grained control over `itemize`, `enumerate`, and `description` lists, including margins, item separation, and label formats.
details:
`enumitem` is the modern way to customise lists. It lets you pass key–value options to `itemize`, `enumerate`, and `description`: `\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, topsep=0pt]`. The keys include `label`, `labelsep`, `leftmargin`, `itemindent`, `itemsep`, `parsep`, `topsep`, `partopsep`, `start` (for `enumerate`), `resume` (continue numbering from a previous list), and `nosep` (a shortcut for zero spacing).

For `enumerate`, you can change the label format with `label=\alph*)`, `label=\Roman*.`, etc., and `\begin{enumerate}[resume]` continues numbering across interrupted lists — a feature that plain LaTeX lacks. You can also define reusable list styles with `\newlist{myitems}{itemize}{1}` and `\setlist[myitems]{label=\textbullet, leftmargin=*}`.

`enumitem` must be loaded after `babel` and `hyperref` in some cases (its documentation recommends loading it last if you have conflicts). It also has a `shortlabels` option that enables the `[(a)]` style of shorthand labels from the old `enumerate` package. It does not support the `amsthm` theorem lists directly, but you can combine it with `amsthm` for theorem-like lists. If you use `beamer`, note that `beamer` has its own list customisation — avoid loading `enumitem` with it.

name: caption
desc: Offers many ways to format captions in figures and tables, including font, label separator, and justification. It also cooperates with `subcaption`.
details:
`caption` provides a uniform way to style all captions in your document. You set options globally with `\captionsetup{font=small, labelfont=bf, labelsep=period, justification=raggedright}` and can override them per-float with `\captionsetup[figure]{...}` or locally with `\captionsetup{...}` inside a float. The options cover font (`font=small|footnotesize|...`), label font and separator (`labelsep=colon|period|space|quad`), justification, indentation, and single-line behaviour.

It also provides the `\captionof{float}{text}` command for adding a caption outside a float — useful for non-floating tables or `minipage` figures. The package handles the interaction with `hyperref` correctly, so captions remain clickable, and it plays well with `subcaption` (which itself requires `caption`).

One important interaction: `caption` redefines `\caption` and `\captionof`; if another package also patches them (e.g. some journal classes), load order matters. It is generally safe to load `caption` early in the preamble. If you need captions with no label at all, use `labelformat=empty`. If you need to change the caption of the list of figures, combine `caption` with `tocloft`.

name: float
desc: Provides the `[H]` placement option to force a float to appear exactly where it is written, and improves the interface for defining new float types.
details:
`float` provides the much-loved `[H]` specifier, which forces a float to appear exactly at the point where it is written in the source — effectively turning it into a non-floating block with a caption. It is the go-to fix when you need a figure or table to stay put (e.g. a figure that must be next to the paragraph that discusses it). Usage: `\begin{figure}[H] ... \end{figure}`.

The package also improves the interface for defining new float types with `\newfloat{type}{placement}{ext}{within}` and `\floatname{type}{Name}`, and it provides `\floatstyle{plain|boxed|ruled}` for consistent float styling. The `[H]` option is implemented by temporarily disabling the float mechanism, so the object is placed exactly where it appears in the source, and page breaking may occur awkwardly around it.

Using `[H]` too often defeats LaTeX's float placement algorithm, which is designed to avoid large white gaps. Prefer `[htbp]` in normal writing and reserve `[H]` for cases where the exact position really matters. Also, `[H]` floats cannot be moved, so a large `[H]` figure near the bottom of a page can leave a big blank space. Combine with `placeins` if you want to keep floats within sections without forcing exact positions.

name: placeins
desc: Defines `\FloatBarrier` to prevent floats from moving past a certain point, ensuring that all figures and tables stay within their section.
details:
`placeins` solves the problem of floats drifting into a later section than the one they belong to. You insert `\FloatBarrier` at the end of a section, and LaTeX will flush all pending floats before continuing, so no float can appear after the barrier. This is exactly what you want at the end of a chapter, or before a section that should start with a clean page.

The package option `section` (i.e. `\usepackage[section]{placeins}`) automatically inserts a barrier at every `\section`, which is often all you need. There is also a `below` option that inserts a barrier before every section. The command `\FloatBarrier` is harmless if there are no pending floats, so it is safe to sprinkle it at strategic points.

A word of caution: `\FloatBarrier` forces floats to be placed *now*, which can produce large white gaps if a float does not fit on the current page. Use it sparingly — the float placement algorithm usually does a good job, and barriers are a corrective tool for when it does not. Also, `\FloatBarrier` has no effect on `[H]` floats from the `float` package, which are already placed exactly.

name: wrapfig
desc: Allows a figure to be placed inside a paragraph with text flowing around it. Useful for small illustrations.
details:
`wrapfig` provides the `wrapfigure` (and `wraptable`) environments, which place a figure or table at the side of a paragraph and let the text flow around it. The syntax is `\begin{wrapfigure}{r}{0.4\textwidth} ... \end{wrapfigure}`, where `r`/`l` is the side, and the width is how much horizontal space the figure occupies. The optional `[lines]` argument controls how many lines of text are shortened.

This is most useful for small illustrations — a logo, a small diagram, or a portrait — where you want text beside the image rather than above and below. It works best when placed at the start of a paragraph, and the figure should be small enough that the wrapped text is readable.

`wrapfig` is notoriously fragile: it does not work inside lists, minipages, or other floats, and it interacts poorly with page breaks. The number of shortened lines is estimated, and you often need to tweak it manually. It also does not work with `\parbox`/`minipage`-like content. For robust results, place a `wrapfigure` at the beginning of a paragraph, use a width less than `0.5\textwidth`, and compile twice to let the line count settle. If it misbehaves, consider `
\begin{minipage}` with `\parbox` as a fallback.

name: subcaption
desc: Provides the `subfigure` and `subtable` environments, along with `\subcaption` and `\subref`, to create and reference sub‑floats within a larger float.
details:
`subcaption` is the modern, recommended way to create sub-figures and sub-tables. Inside a `figure` you place several `\begin{subfigure}{0.45\textwidth} ... \end{subfigure}` blocks, each with its own `\subcaption` and `\label`. The outer `figure` has a main `\caption`; the sub-figures get (a), (b), (c) labels automatically, and `\subref{...}` produces just the letter for inline references.

This replaces the older `subfigure` and `subfig` packages (both have similar names but different syntax). The `subcaption` package is built on top of `caption`, so the two work together; it is generally best to load `caption` then `subcaption`. The sub-figure width should be chosen so the blocks fit in a row; use `\hfill` or `\hspace` between them.

A common pattern is `\begin{figure} \centering \begin{subfigure}{0.45\textwidth} \includegraphics{...} \caption{...} \label{fig:a} \end{subfigure} \hfill \begin{subfigure}{0.45\textwidth} ... \end{subfigure} \caption{Overall} \label{fig:both} \end{figure}`. You can also use `\subcaptionbox{...}{...}` for a one-off. The package requires `caption`, and works with `hyperref` for clickable sub-references.

name: listings
desc: Includes program listings with syntax highlighting, line numbers, and captions. It is fully integrated with LaTeX and does not require external tools.
details:
`listings` is the classic package for typesetting source code. You can include external files with `\lstinputlisting[language=Python]{script.py}` or inline code with `\begin{lstlisting}[language=C] ... \end{lstlisting}`. Options control line numbers (`numbers=left`), frames (`frame=single`), captions (`caption={...}`), and syntax highlighting for dozens of languages.

Its big advantage is that it is pure TeX: no external tools, no shell-escape, works everywhere, and integrates cleanly with `hyperref` and `caption`. You can define your own languages with `\lstdefinelanguage`, style keywords/strings/comments, and set global defaults with `\lstset{...}`.

`listings` has some limitations: its syntax highlighting is regex-based and can be fooled by complex code (e.g. nested strings), it does not handle Unicode well in pdfLaTeX (it needs `extendedchars` and a suitable font), and it cannot break long lines by default (use `breaklines=true`). For fancier highlighting and Unicode/ligature support, `minted` (which uses Pygments) is the alternative, at the cost of `-shell-escape` and Python. Many authors use `listings` for compatibility and `minted` for showcase-quality output.

name: minted
desc: Uses the Pygments library to provide expressive syntax highlighting for many programming languages. It requires the `-shell-escape` option and Python/Pygments installed.
details:
`minted` uses the Python library Pygments to highlight code, giving richer, more accurate results than the regex-based `listings`. It handles hundreds of languages, supports Unicode naturally, and provides detailed token-level styling. You use `\begin{minted}{python} ... \end{minted}` for inline blocks or `\inputminted{python}{file.py}` for external files, and customise the style with `\usemintedstyle{friendly}` etc.

The cost is a hard dependency: you must compile with `-shell-escape` (so TeX can call Python), have Python and Pygments installed, and the first compilation is slow because Pygments processes the code. `minted` caches its results, so subsequent runs are faster. It works with `hyperref` and `caption` for captions and line numbers (`linenos` option).

Because of the external dependency, `minted` is not ideal for locked-down or minimal TeX installations, or for journals that do not enable `-shell-escape`. It also does not work well with `latexmk` unless you add `-shell-escape` to the command. The output quality is excellent for showcasing code in slides, books, or documentation. If your environment cannot support it, use `listings` with a customised style instead.

name: algorithm2e
desc: Provides a floating `algorithm` environment with predefined keywords (if, while, for, etc.) and customizable typography for pseudocode.
details:
`algorithm2e` is a full-featured package for writing pseudocode. It provides a floating `algorithm` environment and keyword commands like `\If`, `\While`, `\For`, `\KwIn`, `\KwOut`, `\Return`, and `\SetKwFunction`, so the control flow reads naturally. You can choose between several styles (e.g. `ruled`, `boxed`, `linesnumbered`) to match your document's visual language.

A typical algorithm looks like `\begin{algorithm} \caption{My algorithm} \KwIn{$n$} \KwOut{result} \While{condition}{ do something \; } \Return result \end{algorithm}`. The semicolons (`\;`) terminate lines, and the package takes care of indentation, keyword highlighting, and line numbering. You can define your own keywords with `\SetKwInput`, `\SetKw`, and friends.

`algorithm2e` is one of several algorithm packages, alongside `algorithmicx`/`algpseudocode` and `algorithmic`. Each has a different syntax and style; choose one and stick with it. `algorithm2e` is powerful and highly customisable but its syntax is distinctive (keywords rather than an `algorithmic` environment). It works with `hyperref` for clickable algorithm references. If you need a simple numbered pseudocode block without floating, you can use it inside a `minipage` or `algorithm*` to suppress the float.

name: babel
desc: Adapts LaTeX to the typographic and hyphenation rules of many languages. Load it with the desired language option (e.g., `\usepackage[english]{babel}`).
details:
`babel` adapts LaTeX to the conventions of a particular language: hyphenation patterns, quotation marks, the words for "Figure", "Table", "Contents", date formats, and the placement of punctuation around maths. Load it with language options, e.g. `\usepackage[english,ngerman]{babel}` — the last language is the main one, and `\selectlanguage{...}` switches mid-document.

The package also provides shortcuts for language-specific characters. For example, with `[ngerman]`, `"a` produces ä; with `[french]`, `\fg` etc. `\usepackage[english,french]{babel}` plus `\selectlanguage{french}` is enough to typeset a bilingual document. It also defines `\foreignlanguage{french}{...}` for short switching.

`babel` is one of the most widely used packages and has extensive language coverage, but with pdfLaTeX it needs `inputenc`/`fontenc` to handle accented input, and with XeLaTeX/LuaLaTeX you often want `fontspec` and possibly `polyglossia` instead. Its `french` option famously changes spacing around punctuation (a thin space before `:` and `;`); this is correct typography but can surprise people. Load `babel` early and, if you also use `csquotes`, let it detect the language automatically.

name: inputenc
desc: Tells LaTeX which character encoding the source file uses (e.g., `\usepackage[utf8]{inputenc}`). With XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX, UTF‑8 is native, so this package is usually unnecessary.
details:
`inputenc` tells pdfLaTeX how to interpret the bytes of your source file. The recommended option is `utf8`, which lets you type accented characters and other Unicode directly: `\usepackage[utf8]{inputenc}` then `café` in the source produces the correct output (provided the font has the glyph). Without it, pdfLaTeX assumes a single-byte encoding and will produce garbled output or errors on non-ASCII characters.

Under XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX, UTF-8 is the native input encoding, so `inputenc` is unnecessary and in fact not recommended — those engines handle Unicode directly, and loading `inputenc` can cause conflicts. For pdfLaTeX, `utf8` is the modern default and is essentially always what you want.

When you use `inputenc` with pdfLaTeX, you also need `fontenc` (typically `[T1]`) to get proper glyphs and hyphenation for accented characters. The combination `\usepackage[utf8]{inputenc} \usepackage[T1]{fontenc}` is the classic pdfLaTeX preamble for European languages. If you use XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX, skip `inputenc` and use `fontspec` with a Unicode font instead.

name: fontenc
desc: Selects the font encoding (e.g., `\usepackage[T1]{fontenc}`) to enable proper hyphenation and access to accented characters in the output.
details:
`fontenc` selects the font encoding used in the output. The default for pdfLaTeX is OT1, which is fine for pure English but has poor support for accented characters and gives no hyphenation of words containing them. `\usepackage[T1]{fontenc}` switches to the T1 encoding, which supports the full Latin alphabet (including accented letters as single glyphs), proper hyphenation, and better kerning.

With T1, the standard Computer Modern fonts are replaced by a T1-compatible variant; you often want to load `lmodern` at the same time so the result looks right. The T1 encoding is what most modern documents use. For Cyrillic or Greek, you would use `[T2A]` or `[LGR]` with the appropriate font packages (e.g. `babel` language support).

`fontenc` is only relevant for pdfLaTeX. With XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX, font encoding is handled by `fontspec` and the OpenType font itself, so `fontenc` is not needed and should not be loaded. A common mistake is loading `fontenc` with XeLaTeX, which can cause warnings or font substitution problems. Another is forgetting `fontenc` with pdfLaTeX and then wondering why copy-pasting from the PDF gives mojibake for accented letters.

name: lmodern
desc: Loads the Latin Modern family, a high‑quality extension of Computer Modern with improved glyph coverage. It is a safe default for many documents.
details:
`lmodern` loads the Latin Modern family, which is a Unicode-era extension of Computer Modern (the default LaTeX font). It provides the familiar CM look but with better glyph coverage, improved hinting, and OpenType versions for XeLaTeX/LuaLaTeX. Loading it gives you consistent text and maths fonts and, crucially, the T1-encoded version of Computer Modern when used with `fontenc`.

Under pdfLaTeX, the combination `\usepackage[T1]{fontenc} \usepackage{lmodern}` is a very common preamble: it produces a document that looks like standard LaTeX but has proper accented characters, correct hyphenation, and scalable fonts (instead of the bitmap versions that pdfLaTeX would otherwise use). Under XeLaTeX/LuaLaTeX you can load `lmodern` and/or `fontspec` with `\setmainfont{Latin Modern Roman}`.

One subtlety: `lmodern` is not mandatory if you use `fontspec` with a system font; in that case, the fontspec font overrides Latin Modern. If you like the CM look but want higher quality, `newpx`/`newtx` (Palatino/Times-like) or `libertinus` are alternatives. For maths, `lmodern` is a safe default but `mathpazo`, `newtxmath`, or `unicode-math` may be preferred for specific styles.

name: microtype
desc: Enables character protrusion and font expansion (with pdfTeX) to reduce overfull lines and improve the visual appearance of paragraphs.
details:
`microtype` implements micro-typographic refinements that make a noticeable difference in output quality. It adds **character protrusion** (hyphens and punctuation hang slightly into the margin) and **font expansion** (glyphs are stretched or shrunk by a tiny amount so that a line fits without an overfull box). The result is fewer overfull lines, fewer hyphens, and a more even text block.

Usage is trivial: `\usepackage{microtype}`. There are options to control how aggressive the protrusion and expansion are, and you can disable them individually (`protrusion=false`, `expansion=false`). Under pdfTeX, font expansion requires the fonts to support it; the default settings are conservative and safe. Under XeLaTeX, only protrusion is available (no font expansion); under LuaLaTeX, both work but with some font limitations.

`microtype` is one of the few packages that improves typography with essentially no downside. The only caveats: it can slightly change line breaks (usually for the better), and it does not work with some bitmap fonts. It should be loaded last or near-last in the preamble (after `fontenc`/`fontspec`), so it knows the fonts in use. If you are submitting to a journal that forbids it, the difference is subtle but the package is otherwise highly recommended.

name: parskip
desc: Creates a layout with no paragraph indentation and a non‑zero vertical space between paragraphs, which is common in web‑style or modern documents.
details:
`parskip` changes the paragraph style from the classic "indent first line, no vertical space" to "no indent, vertical space between paragraphs". This is the style used by most web content and many modern reports. It is a one-line change: `\usepackage{parskip}` (or `\usepackage[parfill]{parskip}` to also remove the extra space before the first paragraph after a heading).

The package does more than just set `\parindent=0pt` and `\parskip=...`; it also adjusts the spacing around lists, floats, and displayed equations to stay consistent, which is why loading it is preferable to manually redefining the lengths. It is especially useful in documents where paragraphs are short and separation is important (letters, web-style reports, some theses).

Some publishing houses and journals expect the classical indented style, so check your template. In `book`-like classes, `parskip` can interfere with the chapter-opening layout if loaded before the class option `parskip` is used. Modern KOMA-Script classes have a `parskip` class option that is more deeply integrated. For a quick visual change, `\usepackage{parskip}` is hard to beat.

name: ragged2e
desc: Provides `\RaggedRight`, `\RaggedLeft`, and `\Centering` that allow hyphenation while still producing ragged margins, unlike the standard `\raggedright`.
details:
`ragged2e` improves on LaTeX's built-in ragged-right commands. The built-in `\raggedright` disables hyphenation, which produces very ragged edges and wastes space. `ragged2e`'s `\RaggedRight` keeps hyphenation enabled while still typesetting with a ragged right edge, giving a much more balanced appearance. The family includes `\RaggedLeft`, `\Centering`, `\RaggedRightParindent`, and environments `\begin{RaggedRight} ... \end{RaggedRight}`.

The package also provides `\SetRaggedRight` and length parameters (`\RaggedRightRightskip`, etc.) to tune how ragged the text is, and a `\Centering` that respects paragraph indentation. It works well in narrow columns (e.g. in `tabularx` tables, `minipage`s) where justified text produces huge inter-word gaps.

Typical use is `\usepackage{ragged2e}` then `\RaggedRight` before a narrow block, or `>{\RaggedRight\arraybackslash}X` in a `tabularx` column. The `\arraybackslash` is required because `\RaggedRight` redefines `\\`. The `ragged2e` package is a strict improvement over the built-in commands and is widely used in professional typesetting for narrow measures. If you want justified text but with less hyphenation, this is not the package — look at `microtype`'s expansion instead.

name: multicol
desc: Defines the `multicols` environment to typeset text in two or more columns, with automatic balancing at the end.
details:
`multicol` provides the `multicols` environment for multi-column text. `\begin{multicols}{2} ... \end{multicols}` lays out the content in two balanced columns, with column breaks determined automatically. It balances the columns at the end (unless you use `multicols*`, which does not balance). You can insert manual breaks with `\columnbreak` and force a page break with `\newpage`.

The package handles floats awkwardly: floats inside `multicols` are not supported in the usual way (a single `figure` in a two-column layout floats to the top of the current column, but the behaviour is limited). For two-column documents with full-width floats, the standard solution is the document class's two-column option (`\documentclass[twocolumn]{article}`) or the `cuted` package for full-width content inside `multicols`. `multicol` also supports a `\begin{multicols}{2}[\section{...}]` optional argument for a title spanning all columns.

`multicol` is robust and widely used for newsletters, proceedings, and boxed multi-column content. It does not interact with `hyperref` badly, but references inside it are fine. For a balanced two-column layout of a long text, `multicol` is the simplest tool. For magazine-style layouts with full-width headers and figures, a class or `flowfram`/`tcolorbox` combination is more appropriate.

name: natbib
desc: Provides flexible citation commands (e.g., `\citep`, `\citet`) for author–year and numerical references, and works with many BibTeX styles.
details:
`natbib` provides author–year citations on top of BibTeX. The two key commands are `\citet{key}` (textual: "Jones (2020) showed…") and `\citep{key}` (parenthetical: "…(Jones, 2020)"). It also provides `\citeauthor`, `\citeyear`, `\citeyearpar`, and `\citetext`, and supports numerical citations with `\cite`-style output when used with a numeric style.

It is a front-end to the BibTeX styles: use `\bibliographystyle{plainnat}` (or `apalike`, `abbrvnat`, etc.) and `\bibliography{refs}`. `natbib` also supports multiple keys (`\citep{a,b,c}`), sorting and compressing numeric citations (with the `sort&compress` option), and the `\setcitestyle` command to configure punctuation and brackets. It works well with `hyperref` (clickable citations) and with `babel`/`csquotes` for language-specific "and"/"&" output.

`natbib` is the traditional choice and remains widely used in the sciences. Its main competitor is `biblatex` (with `biber`), which is more modern and flexible but is a full replacement rather than a front-end. If you are writing a journal article with an existing `.bst` style, `natbib` is often required. If you are starting fresh, `biblatex` may be more future-proof. Do not load `natbib` and `biblatex` together — they are incompatible.

name: biblatex
desc: A complete reimplementation of LaTeX’s bibliography facilities, with full Unicode support, flexible sorting, and many citation styles. It requires the `biber` backend.
details:
`biblatex` is a complete rewrite of LaTeX's bibliography handling. Instead of `.bst` files and BibTeX, it uses `biber` as the backend and `biblatex`'s own styles. You load it with `\usepackage[style=authoryear]{biblatex}`, add `\addbibresource{refs.bib}`, and print the bibliography with `\printbibliography`. Citation commands are `\cite`, `\parencite`, `\textcite`, `\autocite`, `\footcite`, and many more, and the output adapts to the chosen style.

The big advantages are: full Unicode support (no more fighting with BibTeX over accents), flexible sorting and filtering (`\nocite`, `\printbibliography[type=article]`), per-entry data model customisation, and dozens of styles covering APA, Chicago, MLA, numeric, and verbose forms. `biber` also understands crossrefs, related entries, and date ranges. Because it is all driven by `biblatex`, changing citation style is a one-line change.

The cost is that you must compile with `biber` (not `bibtex`), which means running `pdflatex` → `biber` → `pdflatex` → `pdflatex`. This is automated by `latexmk -pdf`. `biblatex` is incompatible with `natbib`; if your journal requires `.bst` styles, you cannot use `biblatex`. It is, however, the recommended modern choice for theses and books where you control the whole toolchain.

name: cite
desc: Enhances numerical citations by supporting compressed, sorted lists (e.g., `[1–3]`) and better handling of punctuation and line breaks.
details:
The `cite` package improves the appearance of numeric citations in BibTeX-based documents. Its headline feature is **compression**: `\cite{a,b,c}` where the keys are numbered 1, 2, 3 produces `[1–3]` rather than `[1,2,3]`. It also sorts the keys so the output is always in numeric order, and it handles punctuation and line breaks around citations better than the standard `\cite`.

It works with the standard `\bibliographystyle{plain}` and similar styles; it does not require a special `.bst`. Options include `nocompress` (to disable the range compression), `sort` (to sort), and `move` (to move punctuation). There is also `\citen` for a single reference, `\citeauthor`, and `\citeyear`. The package is small and works with `hyperref` (clickable links) and `natbib` in some configurations (though `natbib` already has its own `sort&compress`).

In modern documents, `natbib` with the `sort&compress` option, or `biblatex` with `style=numeric-comp`, are usually preferred because they are more actively maintained and better integrated. `cite` remains useful in legacy documents that use plain BibTeX and want compression without changing their bibliography style. Its main limitation is that it only handles numeric citations.

name: csquotes
desc: Provides `\enquote` and other commands that automatically use the correct quotation marks for the current language, avoiding manual quote characters.
details:
`csquotes` provides `\enquote{...}`, which typesets quotation marks that are correct for the current language, as determined by `babel` or `polyglossia`. For English it gives “...”, for German „...“, for French «...», and so on. This means you never have to remember or type the raw quote characters — the package handles the style and the surrounding spacing automatically. Nested quotes are handled correctly, too.

The package also provides `\blockquote`, `\blockcquote`, `\foreignquote`, and `\hyphenquote` for longer quotations, and `\textquote` for inline quotes with proper punctuation handling. It works with `biblatex`'s `\blockquote`-style citation commands (e.g. `\blockcquote{key}{...}` prints a quotation and cites its source).

`csquotes` should be loaded after `babel`/`polyglossia`, so it can detect the language. It also provides the `autostyle` option to enable automatic quotation style per language. Its greatest benefit is consistency: every quotation in the document uses the same style, and switching the document language switches the quote style automatically. It is often used with `biblatex` for quoting sources in humanities documents. It does not work with XeLaTeX's Unicode quotes unless you set the appropriate style, so check the documentation for your language.

name: glossaries
desc: Helps create and maintain glossaries, acronym lists, and symbol lists, with automatic sorting and linking. It requires an external makeindex run.
details:
`glossaries` manages glossaries, acronym lists, symbol lists, and similar reference sections. You define entries in the preamble with `\newglossaryentry{key}{name={...}, description={...}}` or `\newacronym{key}{short}{long}`, then use `\gls{key}`, `\acrshort{key}`, `\acrlong{key}`, etc. in the text. The package builds the sorted, formatted lists and makes the terms clickable via `hyperref`.

The workflow requires running `makeglossaries` (a Perl script) between LaTeX runs, which calls `makeindex` or `xindy` on the generated files. `\makeglossaries` and `\printglossaries` go in the preamble and at the point where you want the list. With `xindy` you get better sorting and Unicode support; with `makeindex` you get a more portable setup.

The package can also track whether an acronym has been used (so the first use expands it and later uses are short), and it supports plural forms, symbols, and multiple glossaries. It is heavier than `acronym` but much more capable. It plays well with `hyperref` and `babel`, but the external tool chain means your editor or build system must run `makeglossaries`. A common alternative is `glossaries-extra`, which extends it with even more features.

name: acronym
desc: Provides tools to define and use acronyms consistently, including automatic expansion on first use and a printable list of acronyms.
details:
`acronym` is a lightweight package focused on acronyms. You define them with `\acro{API}{Application Programming Interface}` and use `\ac{API}` in the text. On first use, `\ac` prints the full form plus the acronym ("Application Programming Interface (API)"); on later uses, it prints just the acronym. `\acf`, `\acs`, `\acl` force the full, short, or long form; `\acp` gives the plural. A list of acronyms is printed with `\printacronyms` (via `\begin{acronym} ... \end{acronym}`).

The package provides an environment (`acronym`) that acts as the list, and each `\acro` inside it defines an entry. Alternatively you can define acronyms in the preamble and print a list elsewhere. The list is sorted alphabetically when compiled with the right options.

`acronym` is simpler than `glossaries` and requires no external tools, but it is less flexible: it does not support symbols, multiple glossaries, or the same rich formatting. It is a good choice when you only need acronyms. For a modern all-in-one solution (glossary + acronyms + symbols + index), use `glossaries` or `glossaries-extra` instead. If you are writing a short paper, `acronym` is often sufficient and much easier to set up.

name: nomencl
desc: Creates a nomenclature (list of symbols) with automatic sorting and referencing. It works with `makeindex`.
details:
`nomencl` produces a nomenclature — the list of symbols, units, and their definitions that appears in many theses and technical reports. You declare symbols inline with `\nomenclature{$x$}{position}` and print the list with `\printnomenclature`. The entries can be grouped and sorted, and the package generates the file that `makeindex` (or `xindy`) processes.

The workflow is: run LaTeX, then `makeindex <jobname>.nlo -s nomencl.ist -o <jobname>.nls`, then LaTeX again. Many editors and `latexmk` can automate this. The package supports grouping by prefix (`\nomenclature[g]{...}{...}` sorts by the optional first argument), unit columns, and custom formatting.

`nomencl` is the traditional tool for symbol lists; `glossaries` can do the same job with more features and a uniform interface for acronyms, symbols, and glossary terms. If your document already uses `glossaries` for acronyms, you may prefer to add symbols there rather than loading `nomencl`. If you only need a symbol list, `nomencl` is smaller and very focused. Be aware that `nomencl` uses `makeindex` by default and the sorting is ASCII-based, so Greek and other non-Latin symbols need `xindy` or careful prefixing.

name: makeidx
desc: Provides the basic `\makeindex` command and the `theindex` environment to produce an index. It is often used together with `imakeidx` for more control.
details:
`makeidx` is the minimal index package. It provides `\makeindex` (which must be in the preamble) and `\printindex` (which prints the index), plus the `\index{...}` command for marking entries. You write `\index{word}` in the text, run `makeindex` on the generated `.idx` file, and `\printindex` prints the sorted index with page numbers.

The syntax supports subentries with `\index{word!subword}`, cross-references with `\index{word|see{other}}`, page ranges, and formatting. `\index{word|textbf}` prints bold page numbers, for instance. The entries are sorted by `makeindex` using a configuration file; for non-English sorting, you need a custom `.ist` file or `xindy`.

`makeidx` is very small and has no frills. The better modern choice is `imakeidx`, which is a drop-in extension of `makeidx` (you can keep using `\makeindex`) but adds features like automatic `makeindex` runs (via `-shell-escape`), multiple indexes, and finer control. If you are just writing a short document with a small index, `makeidx` is sufficient, but `imakeidx` is usually worth loading instead.

name: imakeidx
desc: Extends `makeidx` with features such as multiple indexes, automatic `makeindex` execution, and finer control over index formatting.
details:
`imakeidx` is a drop-in replacement for `makeidx` that adds important features. The biggest is automatic index generation: with `-shell-escape`, `imakeidx` runs `makeindex` (or `xindy`) for you during the LaTeX run, so you do not need to remember the external step. It also supports **multiple indexes**: `\makeindex[name=authors,title={Author Index}]` and `\index[authors]{...}`, each printed with `\printindex[authors]`.

Other features include per-index sorting and formatting options, `\indexsetup` for configuring the visual style, and the ability to create an index that respects `hyperref` links (clickable page numbers). The `intoc` option adds the index to the table of contents, and `columns` sets the number of columns. It also provides a convenient `\splitindex` mechanism for very large indexes.

`imakeidx` is the recommended choice in modern documents. Its automatic execution relies on `-shell-escape`, so if your build system disables that, it falls back to the manual `makeindex` step. It is compatible with `hyperref`, `babel`, and `glossaries`. If you use `xindy` for Unicode sorting, `imakeidx` handles the invocation transparently. For a document with several indexes (author, subject, symbol), `imakeidx` is significantly easier than `makeidx`.

name: todonotes
desc: Adds coloured margin notes (e.g., `\todo{...}`) to mark unfinished work or reminders. It can also produce a list of all todos.
details:
`todonotes` lets you attach margin notes to mark unfinished work. The main command is `\todo{Remember to add a citation here}`, which prints a coloured note in the margin (or inline, with `inline` option) and draws a line to the anchor point. You can style the notes with `\todo[color=red, size=\small, inline]{...}` and add a `\listoftodos` to collect all open items.

It is a practical tool during drafting: you can leave notes to yourself or co-authors, and they are visually obvious so they will not be forgotten. Options include `disable` (to hide all notes for a clean final version without deleting them), `french`/`ngerman` for localised default text, and `obeyDraft` to print notes only in draft mode (using the `draft` class option).

The package depends on `tikz` (for the visual style) and `xcolor`. It can conflict with other margin-note packages (`marginnote`, `sidenotes`), so use one at a time. In the final version, `\usepackage[disable]{todonotes}` turns all `\todo` commands into no-ops, which is cleaner than deleting them. For a more flexible alternative, `pdfcomment` provides PDF annotations, and `marginnote` is a lower-level tool.

name: tocloft
desc: Allows you to change the appearance of the table of contents, list of figures, and list of tables (spacing, fonts, dotted lines, etc.).
details:
`tocloft` customises the table of contents, list of figures, and list of tables. You can adjust the font and size of the title (`\renewcommand{\cfttoctitlefont}{\Large\bfseries}`), the indentation of entries (`\setlength{\cftsecindent}{0pt}`), the spacing between entries, and the style of the dotted leaders (`\renewcommand{\cftdot}{.}` or `\renewcommand{\cftdotsep}{...}`).

The package groups its settings by level: `\cftchapfont`, `\cftchappagefont`, `\cftsecfont`, `\cftsubsecindent`, and so on for chapter, section, subsection, figure, table, and their page numbers. This makes it easy to set a consistent visual hierarchy. You can also add extra space around a level with `\cftbeforechapskip`, and control whether leaders appear with `\cftsecleader`.

It works with the standard classes and is compatible with `hyperref` and `titlesec` (which handles the section headings themselves). One caveat: if you also use `titletoc` (from the `titlesec` author), that package has overlapping functionality and they may conflict. `tocloft` is the standard choice for fine-tuning the TOC without changing the section heading style. For adding unnumbered entries or changing the TOC title in `book` classes, it provides `\cftaddtitleline` and related commands.

name: appendix
desc: Provides the `\appendix` command and the `appendices` environment to switch to appendix numbering (A, B, C…) for chapters or sections.
details:
The `appendix` package provides a more robust `\appendix` mechanism than the built-in command. It offers the `appendices` environment and `\appendixpage` (which prints an "Appendices" title page), and it switches numbering to A, B, C… for chapters or sections, depending on the class. It also redefines `\thechapter`/`\thesection` so that references and the TOC pick up the new numbering correctly.

The package's advantage over the built-in `\appendix` is that it handles the `book`/`report` classes more cleanly: chapters after `\appendix` are numbered A, B, C and their subsections A.1, A.2, while the chapter title itself is still formatted as a chapter. It also interacts correctly with `hyperref` (bookmarks) and `cleveref` (references to appendices).

Usage is simple: after your main content, write `\appendix` (or `\begin{appendices} ... \end{appendices}`), and subsequent `\chapter`/`\section` commands will be numbered with letters. If you want a separate "Appendices" page, use `\appendixpage`. Note that `appendix` can conflict with `titlesec` or `tocloft` if they are loaded and also patch the same commands; check the load order. In KOMA-Script and `memoir`, the built-in mechanisms are usually preferred.

name: etoolbox
desc: Offers a large collection of programming utilities (e.g., `\ifundef`, `\patchcmd`, list processing) that are useful for writing robust LaTeX code.
details:
`etoolbox` is a Swiss-army knife for LaTeX programming. It provides `\patchcmd` (to safely modify an existing macro), `\ifundef`, `\ifdef`, `\ifcsdef` (conditional checks), `\newtoggle`/`\settoggle` (boolean toggles), list processing (`\docsvlist`, `\forcsvlist`, `\listadd`), and robust `\AtBeginEnvironment`/`\AtEndEnvironment` hooks. It also has `\appto`, `\eappto`, and `\gappto` for appending to macros.

For package authors and advanced users, `\patchcmd{\somecommand}{search}{replace}{success}{failure}` is invaluable: it lets you modify a package's command without copying its entire definition. The `\ifundef` and `\ifdef` conditionals are safer and more readable than `\ifx` gymnastics. The toggles are useful for features you want to enable/disable.

`etoolbox` is a dependency of many packages (`biblatex`, `tcolorbox`, `mdframed`, etc.), so it is often already loaded. It works with pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX, and LuaLaTeX. Its list-processing commands are especially handy for iterating over comma-separated data. If you are writing a class or package, `etoolbox` (often together with `xparse`) is the standard modern toolkit. Its `\AtBeginDocument` and environment hooks are more robust than the built-in `\AtBeginDocument` because they work with `\begin{...}` patches.

name: xparse
desc: Provides a modern interface (`\NewDocumentCommand`) for defining commands with optional arguments, stars, and other advanced features.
details:
`xparse` (now part of the LaTeX kernel as the `xparse` module) provides a modern, readable way to define commands with complex argument specs. Instead of `\newcommand` and manual `\@ifstar` tricks, you write `\NewDocumentCommand{\mycmd}{s o m}{...}` where `s` is a star, `o` is an optional argument, and `m` is a mandatory argument. The arguments become `#1`, `#2`, `#3` inside the body, and you can test the star with `\IfBooleanTF`.

The argument spec covers `m` (mandatory), `o` (optional, no default), `O{default}` (optional with default), `s` (star), `d<>` (delimited), `r<>` (required delimited), `v` (verbatim), `t` (token), and more. It also supports processors via `>{...}` and `\ProcessList`, and commands with a `+` prefix to allow paragraphs. `\RenewDocumentCommand`, `\ProvideDocumentCommand`, and `\DeclareDocumentCommand` are the corresponding variants.

`xparse` is essential for package authors and anyone defining a macro with optional arguments and a star. It is more readable than the old `\@ifnextchar` approach, and it produces better error messages. Since 2020 it is part of the LaTeX kernel, so you can use `\NewDocumentCommand` without loading anything in a current TeX distribution — but loading `xparse` is still fine and documents the intent. It pairs naturally with `etoolbox` for robust patching.

name: pgf
desc: The underlying portable graphics format used by TikZ. Most users interact with it through TikZ, but it can also be used directly for advanced graphics programming.
details:
`pgf` (Portable Graphics Format) is the low-level graphics engine that powers `tikz`. It provides the fundamental drawing primitives (`\pgfpathmoveto`, `\pgfpathlineto`, `\pgfusepath`, `\pgfdeclareimage`, etc.), coordinate transformations, and a driver abstraction layer that translates its commands into PDF, PostScript, or SVG output. Most users never touch `pgf` directly because `tikz` wraps it in a much friendlier syntax.

You would use `pgf` directly in advanced scenarios: declaring reusable images, implementing a custom graphics package, or writing code that needs precise control over the drawing state. `pgf` also provides the `\pgfmath` engine (used by `tikz` for calculations), `\pgfkeys` (a powerful key–value parser that many packages use), and `\pgfplots`-compatible math functions.

As an end user, you should almost always load `tikz` (which loads `pgf`) rather than `pgf` alone. Load `pgf` only if you need its low-level features or if you are writing a package that builds on it. `pgf` is very stable and widely used; it is the foundation of most modern LaTeX drawing. The `pgf` manual is huge and detailed — a valuable reference for advanced graphics programming.

name: tikz
desc: A powerful and intuitive language for creating vector graphics (flowcharts, plots, geometric shapes, etc.) directly in LaTeX. It is built on top of PGF.
details:
`tikz` is the dominant drawing package in LaTeX. It provides a high-level, path-based syntax: `\draw (0,0) -- (1,1) -- (2,0);` draws a triangle, `\node at (0,0) {Text};` places a label, and `\fill[red] (0,0) circle (1);` draws a filled circle. Coordinates can be relative (`++`), polar (`(45:2)`), or computed with `\pgfmathparse`. It is built on `pgf` and supports PDF, PostScript, and SVG output.

Beyond basic shapes, `tikz` has libraries for arrows (`arrows.meta`), positioning (`positioning`), trees (`trees`), matrices (`matrix`), calendars, mind maps, and more. You can define styles with `\tikzset{mybox/.style={draw, rounded corners, fill=blue!10}}` and apply them consistently. Nodes can contain text, maths, images, or even other `tikz` pictures, and you can reference them by name (`(a.east)`) for automatic arrow placement.

`tikz` is powerful but can be slow for complex pictures and is not ideal for very data-heavy plots (that is `pgfplots`' job). It integrates beautifully with `beamer` (overlays), `hyperref`, and `babel` (for the `babel` option to make `tikz` shortcuts active). Use `\usetikzlibrary{...}` to load only the libraries you need. For simple diagrams, it is often faster to use a dedicated package (`circuitikz`, `chemfig`) than to draw from scratch.

name: pgfplots
desc: Builds on TikZ to provide a high‑level interface for creating publication‑quality 2D and 3D plots from data or mathematical functions.
details:
`pgfplots` is the standard package for scientific plots in LaTeX. It provides an `axis` environment where you specify the plot directly: `\begin{axis} \addplot {x^2}; \end{axis}`. It supports 2D and 3D plots, logarithmic axes, error bars, bar charts, histograms, contour plots, and even Smith charts. Data can be loaded from files (`\addplot table {data.dat}`) or computed from expressions.

The package has an enormous set of configuration keys: axis labels, ticks, legends, grid, colours, markers, line styles, and per-plot options. You can set global defaults with `\pgfplotsset{compat=1.18, ...}` and override them per axis. It produces vector output, so your plots look great at any zoom level, and the fonts match the rest of the document.

`pgfplots` is slower than exporting a PDF from a plotting tool, especially for large datasets, and complex 3D plots can be very slow or hit TeX's memory limits. For huge datasets, externalisation (`\tikzexternalize`) or pre-processing with `gnuplot` is recommended. Nevertheless, for medium-sized plots and for plots that must match the document's typography exactly, it is the best choice. It is built on `tikz`/`pgf` and shares their coordinate system and styles.

name: tikz-cd
desc: Simplifies the creation of commutative diagrams using TikZ, with a concise syntax and automatic arrow placement.
details:
`tikz-cd` provides a concise syntax for commutative diagrams, which are ubiquitous in category theory, algebra, and topology. Instead of positioning nodes and drawing arrows manually, you write a matrix-like structure: `\begin{tikzcd} A \arrow[r,"f"] \arrow[d,"g"'] & B \arrow[d,"h"] \\ C \arrow[r,"k"'] & D \end{tikzcd}`. The package places the nodes on a grid and draws the arrows automatically.

Arrows can be labelled (`"f"`), dashed, hooked, or two-headed (`\arrow[r, hook]`), and they can be curved (`bend left`), or double (`Rightarrow`). The `'` after a label flips it to the other side. You can also draw arrows between named nodes, add labels above/below, and use `\arrow[dr, dashed]` for diagonal arrows. The package handles alignment, spacing, and scaling for you.

`tikz-cd` is built on `tikz` and requires the `cd` library (loaded automatically). It is far more readable than raw `tikz` for diagrams and produces consistently spaced output. It works well with `amsmath` (for the maths inside) and `hyperref`. For very large or irregular diagrams, raw `tikz` may still be more flexible, but for the typical square or triangular commutative diagram, `tikz-cd` is the standard choice.

name: circuitikz
desc: Provides a set of TikZ commands for drawing electrical and electronic circuits in a clear, standardized way.
details:
`circuitikz` provides a large library of electrical and electronic components for `tikz`: resistors, capacitors, inductors, diodes, transistors, op-amps, logic gates, and many more. You draw a circuit as a path with components inserted along it: `\draw (0,0) to[R, l=$R_1$] (2,0) to[C, l=$C_1$] (2,2);`. The package places the symbol on the path and labels it.

Components have standardised symbols (European or American style, selectable with the `european` option) and can be rotated, mirrored, or given values. You can use `to[short]`, `to[open]`, `to[battery1]`, and hundreds of other component names. The package also supports logic gates (`and port`, `or port`), amplifiers, and switches, and it integrates with `tikz`'s positioning and naming.

`circuitikz` is the go-to package for circuit diagrams in LaTeX, but it has a learning curve: the component library is huge, and finding the exact symbol name can require consulting the manual. For simple circuits, it is very efficient; for complex schematics, a dedicated EDA tool with PDF/SVG export may be faster. It works with `tikz` and `pgf` and is compatible with `beamer` overlays. Load it with `\usepackage[american]{circuitikz}` (or `european`) to choose the symbol style.

name: chemfig
desc: Allows you to draw 2D chemical structures using a simple linear syntax, based on TikZ.
details:
`chemfig` draws 2D chemical structures with a linear, readable syntax. The core command is `\chemfig{...}`, where the structure is written as a sequence of atoms and bonds: `\chemfig{H-O-H}` for water, `\chemfig{-[:30]-[:-30]-[:30]}` for a chain with bond angles. You can build rings with `*6(...)`, add substituents, and label atoms. The package handles bond angles, double/triple bonds, and stereochemistry.

It is built on `tikz`, so you can combine chemical structures with `tikz` annotations, highlight functional groups, or place reaction arrows (`\schemestart ... \arrow ... \schemestop`). The package also provides `\chemname` for names under structures and `\chemabove`/`\chembelow` for labels. There are options for the bond style and the default atom font.

`chemfig` is best for schematic structures with correct angles; for complex natural products or 3D structures, a dedicated drawing tool (ChemDraw, MarvinSketch) exported to PDF is often faster. `chemfig` also does not automatically handle valency or stereochemistry beyond what you specify. For chemical *formulas* and equations, `mhchem` is the right tool — `chemfig` is for drawings, `mhchem` for inline formula text.

name: mhchem
desc: Provides commands for typesetting chemical formulas (e.g., `\ce{H2O}`) and equations with proper formatting of subscripts, charges, and isotopes.
details:
`mhchem` typesets chemical formulas and equations with the correct formatting automatically. The `\ce{...}` command takes a compact syntax and produces a properly formatted formula: `\ce{H2O}` gives H₂O with subscripts, `\ce{Fe^3+}` gives Fe³⁺ with a superscript, and `\ce{^{14}C}` gives the isotope notation.
