It also handles reaction arrows (`->`, `<=>`, `<=>>`), state symbols (`(aq)`, `(s)`), and stoichiometric coefficients.

The package is smart about the conventions: subscripts and superscripts are placed correctly, charges are typeset in the right font, and the spacing around arrows and plus signs is automatic. `\ce{2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O}` produces a properly typeset equation with aligned arrows. It works in both text and maths mode and integrates with `amsmath` for numbered equations.

`mhchem` is compatible with pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX, and LuaLaTeX, and it works well with `siunitx` for physical quantities. It does not draw structures — for that, use `chemfig`. Load it with `\usepackage[version=4]{mhchem}` (the current version) to get the latest syntax. A common use is inside `equation` environments or in tables of chemical data. It is one of those packages that saves enormous time if you write chemistry.

name: physics
desc: Offers concise commands for derivatives, integrals, vectors, matrices, and other physics‑related notation (e.g., `\dv{f}{x}`, `\ev{x}`).
details:
`physics` provides shorthand commands for the notation physicists use constantly. `\dv{f}{x}` typesets df/dx, `\pdv{f}{x}` gives the partial derivative, `\dd` gives the differential d, `\ev{x}` gives ⟨x⟩ (expectation value), `\bra`/`\ket`/`\braket` handle Dirac notation, and `\va`/`\vb`/`\vu` give vectors and unit vectors. It also provides `\qty`, `\abs`, and `\norm` for delimiters.

The package is designed to reduce typing and improve consistency: derivatives, vectors, and bras/kets get the correct spacing and font automatically. It is widely used in physics theses and papers. The commands are usually intuitive and the package documentation is a compact reference.

Caveats: `physics` is no longer actively maintained (the original author stepped away), and it redefines some commands that can clash with other packages. In particular, it can conflict with `siunitx` (both define `\qty`) and `mathtools` (both define `\abs`/`\norm`). If you hit a clash, load `physics` with `\usepackage{physics}` and then re-declare the conflicting commands, or avoid the overlapping ones. For new documents, some authors prefer `physics2` (a fork) or writing the notation manually with `mathtools`. Still, for physics-heavy documents, `physics` is very convenient.

name: cancel
desc: Adds commands to draw a diagonal line through a term in a formula (e.g., `\cancel{x}`), useful for showing simplification.
details:
`cancel` draws a diagonal line through a term in a formula to show that it cancels or is being removed. The commands are `\cancel{...}`, `\bcancel{...}` (backwards diagonal), `\xcancel{...}` (both diagonals, a cross), and `\cancelto{value}{...}` (which draws the cancellation line and places a value above it, e.g. `\cancelto{0}{x}`).

This is useful in worked derivations where a term is eliminated by simplification. For example, `\frac{\cancel{x} y}{\cancel{x} z} = \frac{y}{z}` shows visually that x cancels. The line is drawn with the correct thickness and angle and follows the term's bounding box, so it works with fractions, roots, and symbols.

`cancel` works in both inline and display maths and requires `amsmath` (or just standard maths). It is a small, focused package with no real alternatives (though you could draw the lines with `tikz`, which is overkill). The `\cancelto` variant is especially nice for limits: `\lim_{x \to 0} \cancelto{1}{\frac{\sin x}{x}}`. It is compatible with `hyperref` and other standard packages. If you want to cancel across a whole equation, use it inside `align` with `&` alignment.

name: ulem
desc: Provides commands for underlining, striking out, and adding squiggly lines under text, with options for hyphenation and line breaks.
details:
`ulem` provides underlining that actually works across line breaks and with hyphenation. The standard `\underline` does not break across lines and looks ugly for long text; `ulem`'s `\uline{...}` does break correctly, and it offers `\uuline` (double underline), `\uwave` (wavy underline), `\sout` (strike-through), `\xout` (cross-out), and `\dashuline`/`\dotuline` (dashed/dotted).

The package also lets you customise the underline: `\ULdepth`, `\ULthickness`, and the `normalem` option (which keeps `\emph` italic instead of switching to underline). By default `ulem` redefines `\emph` to underline — which is a legacy behaviour — so most users load it with `\usepackage[normalem]{ulem}` to keep italics.

`ulem` is often used in documents that need true strikethrough or wavy underlines, e.g. for corrections or for linguistic examples. It can conflict with `hyperref` in some versions; load `ulem` before `hyperref` if possible. For highlighting, `soul` is a better choice (it handles colours), but for line-breaking underlines and strike-throughs, `ulem` is the standard. Note that the output is drawn with rules, so the underline may not follow the exact shape of descenders.

name: soul
desc: Enables letter‑spacing, underlining, striking out, and highlighting of text, even across line breaks.
details:
`soul` provides commands that can stretch, underline, strike, and highlight text across line breaks. The main commands are `\so{...}` (letter-spacing), `\ul{...}` (underline), `\st{...}` (strike-through), and `\hl{...}` (highlight, using a colour argument like `\hl[yellow]{...}`). Unlike `ulem`'s rule-based underlines, `soul`'s highlighting actually fills the background, and it handles hyphenation and line breaks correctly.

The package is particularly useful for highlighting text in a way that looks like a marker pen, which `ulem` cannot do (it only draws lines). It also has `\caps` for small caps and `\textso`/`\textul` variants. The colour highlighting uses `xcolor`, so load `xcolor` first. `soul` is efficient and produces good results in most fonts.

The main limitation is that `soul` cannot handle every construct: it does not work inside maths or with verbatim-like content, and very complicated text can produce warnings. For heavy highlighting and letter-spacing, `soul` is still the best choice; `soulutf8` is an extension for Unicode input with pdfLaTeX. Load `soul` after `xcolor`. If you only need occasional highlighting, `\hl` from `soul` is simpler than `tcolorbox` or `colorbox` for inline use.

name: xspace
desc: Automatically inserts a space after a command if the next character is not punctuation, preventing unwanted concatenation.
details:
`xspace` solves a small but annoying problem: when you define a command like `\newcommand{\LaTeX}{\LaTeX\xspace}` or a custom macro ending in a word, you usually want a space after it, but you do not want a space before a following punctuation mark. `\xspace` inserts a space only if the next token is not punctuation, closing brace, or similar.

The classic use is `\newcommand{\myterm}{some term\xspace}` so that `\myterm is` produces "some term is" while `\myterm,` produces "some term," without an extra space before the comma. It is also handy for abbreviations like `\newcommand{\eg}{e.g.\xspace}`. Without `\xspace`, authors often write `\myterm\ ` and get an unwanted space before punctuation.

`xspace` is tiny and works everywhere. The main caveat is that it should be the last thing in a macro, and it does not work correctly when the following text is in a different context (e.g. inside `\section{...}` it can interact with the TOC). It also should not be used at the end of a macro that takes arguments in a way that swallows the following space. Despite these edge cases, it is a very common and useful tool in the preamble of documents that define their own abbreviations.

name: calc
desc: Allows arithmetic expressions (e.g., `\setlength{\parindent}{0.5\textwidth + 1em}`) in places where LaTeX expects a length.
details:
`calc` lets you use arithmetic expressions wherever LaTeX expects a length. Instead of pre-computing values, you write `\setlength{\parindent}{0.5\textwidth + 1em}` or `\includegraphics[width=\textwidth-2cm]{...}`. The package parses the expression and evaluates it using TeX's dimension arithmetic, so you can mix units (cm, pt, em, `\textwidth`) and use `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, and parentheses.

The classic use is adjusting widths: `\parbox{\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule}{...}` or `\begin{minipage}{0.5\textwidth-1cm}`. It also works in `\hspace`, `\vspace`, `\rule`, and any command that takes a length. `calc` redefines the length-parsing internals so the arithmetic works transparently.

`calc` is very old but still works; however, it has some limitations with newer LaTeX features and can conflict with packages that also patch length parsing (e.g. `tabularx` in some versions). Modern alternatives include `\dimexpr` (built into e-TeX, available in pdfLaTeX/XeLaTeX/LuaLaTeX) and `\glueexpr`, which are more robust and do not require a package. For example, `\setlength{\parindent}{\dimexpr 0.5\textwidth + 1em\relax}` works without `calc`. Many authors still load `calc` for convenience, but `\dimexpr` is the modern, conflict-free way.

name: ifthen
desc: Provides `\ifthenelse` and boolean logic for writing conditional statements in LaTeX code.
details:
`ifthen` provides a readable conditional construct: `\ifthenelse{test}{then-code}{else-code}`. The test can compare numbers (`\equal{1}{1}`, `\lengthtest{\linewidth > 10cm}`), strings (`\equal{abc}{abc}`), or booleans (`\boolean{flag}`). You can combine tests with `\and`, `\or`, `\not`, and parentheses, and define new booleans with `\newboolean{flag}` and `\setboolean{flag}{true}`.

This is much more readable than the primitive `\if...\fi` constructs and is useful in the preamble or in macros that need to behave differently based on a condition. For example, `\ifthenelse{\equal{\jobname}{draft}}{\includecomment{...}}{...}` or a macro that prints a value if a flag is set. The package also provides `\whiledo{test}{body}` for loops.

`ifthen` is old but widely used; modern alternatives include `etoolbox`'s `\ifboolexpr` and `\ifdef`, and `xparse`'s argument tests. `ifthen` can be fragile when the test involves complex macros, because it expands them. For simple numeric/string comparisons it is fine. Since it is part of the standard LaTeX distribution, it is always available, but for new code `etoolbox`'s conditionals are generally more robust and powerful. Load it in the preamble; it does not conflict with much.

name: keyval
desc: Provides a simple mechanism for parsing key–value pairs, which is used by many packages to offer flexible options.
details:
`keyval` is the classic package for parsing key–value options. It provides `\define@key{family}{key}{code}` to define a key and `\setkeys{family}{key=value, key2=value2}` to process them. Many packages accept options this way; `keyval` is the underlying machinery for `graphicx`'s `width=...`, `geometry`'s `margin=...`, etc.

For package authors, `keyval` is a simple, dependency-free way to give your commands a flexible interface. You define a family (usually your package name), define each key with its code, and then call `\setkeys`. Keys can be boolean (presence = true) or take values, and you can set defaults with `\define@key` followed by `\setkeys`. It also provides `\@ifundefined`-style checks and `\keyval`-specific commands like `\presetkeys` (from `xkeyval`).

`keyval` has largely been superseded by `pgfkeys` (part of `pgf`), which is far more powerful (it supports handlers, styles, choice keys, and default values), and by `l3keys` in the LaTeX3 kernel. For new package code, `pgfkeys` or `l3keys` is recommended. `keyval` is still used by older packages and is tiny, but its parsing is limited: it does not support comma-separated lists with nested braces elegantly, and error messages are not very helpful. If you are writing a new package, prefer `pgfkeys`.

name: graphics
desc: The original package for including graphics files. Most users use `graphicx` instead, which extends `graphics` with a key–value interface.
details:
`graphics` is the original graphics-inclusion package. It provides `\includegraphics` and the `graphicspath` mechanism, but with a positional-argument interface rather than `graphicx`'s key–value one. For example, `\includegraphics[scale=0.5]{file}` is `graphicx`; the original `graphics` syntax uses `\includegraphics[0,0][2cm,2cm]{file}` (a bounding-box/scale form). It also provides `\rotatebox`, `\scalebox`, and `\resizebox`.

In practice, `graphicx` is a superset of `graphics` and is what virtually everyone uses. It adds the `width=`, `height=`, `angle=`, `trim=`, `clip`, `page=` keys and is what all modern documentation assumes. The only reason to load `graphics` directly is compatibility with a very old package or a class that expects the original interface.

If you find a document loading `graphics`, you can usually replace it with `graphicx` without changing anything else, because `graphicx` is backwards-compatible with the basic `\includegraphics` usage. The two packages are mutually exclusive (loading both is an error). For new documents, always choose `graphicx`. The `graphics` package is still useful as a minimal dependency when you really do not want the key–value overhead, but that is a rare concern.

name: epstopdf
desc: Automatically converts EPS figures to PDF during compilation (with pdfTeX), allowing EPS files to be included in PDF output.
details:
`epstopdf` converts EPS (Encapsulated PostScript) figures to PDF on the fly during compilation with pdfTeX. pdfTeX cannot include EPS files directly, so if you have EPS figures (common from old plotting tools and from `gnuplot`), `epstopdf` lets you write `\includegraphics{figure.eps}` and have it work. It calls Ghostscript to do the conversion and caches the result so subsequent runs are fast.

The package relies on the `epstopdf` script, which is part of TeX Live and MiKTeX, and it may require `-shell-escape` in some configurations (though TeX Live's restricted `\write18` often allows it for `epstopdf` specifically). You can configure the conversion with options like `update`, `prefersd`, `grayscale`, `pdfversion`, and `outdir`. It works transparently with `graphicx`'s `\includegraphics`.

A common issue is that the generated PDF is not in the graphics path or the conversion fails silently; check the log for `epstopdf` messages. On modern systems, it is often easier to convert EPS to PDF once with `epstopdf` or Ghostscript and include the PDF directly, which avoids the per-compile conversion and any shell-escape issues. `epstopdf` is still valuable for legacy document trees where you cannot change the figure files. It is not needed for XeLaTeX (which can handle EPS via a different route) but is specific to pdfLaTeX workflows.

name: subfig
desc: Provides the `\subfloat` command and `subfigure` environment for creating sub‑figures. It is older than `subcaption` but still widely used.
details:
`subfig` is the older package for sub-figures, predating `subcaption`. It provides the `\subfloat[caption]{content}` command, which places a sub-figure with its own label and caption inside a parent `figure`. You typically use `\subfloat[First]{...}` inside a `figure` environment, with `\hfill` between the sub-floats, and reference them via `\subref{...}` (or `\ref` to the sub-label).

It also provides the `\subfloatrow` and `\subref` commands and integrates with `caption` (which `subfig` requires). The package is widely used in older documents and in templates that predate `subcaption`. Its syntax is different from `subcaption`'s: `subfig` uses `\subfloat` with an optional caption argument, whereas `subcaption` uses a `subfigure` environment with `\subcaption`.

For new documents, `subcaption` is preferred: it is more flexible, better maintained, and has a cleaner syntax. `subfig` is still useful if you have an existing document or a template that uses it. The two packages cannot be loaded together (they conflict over the `\subfloat`/`subfigure` names). If you are converting from `subfig` to `subcaption`, the main change is replacing `\subfloat[caption]{content}` with `\begin{subfigure}{width} content \subcaption{caption} \end{subfigure}`.

name: fancyvrb
desc: Extends the standard `verbatim` environment with options for font size, frame, line numbers, and more.
details:
`fancyvrb` extends the `verbatim` environment with a rich set of options: `\begin{Verbatim}[fontsize=\small, frame=single, numbers=left, numbersep=5pt, breaklines=true, showspaces=true, ...]`. It supports line numbers, frames, backgrounds (`bgcolor`), command display, and inline verbatim with `\Verb`. The `Verbatim` environment is the main one; it preserves exact spacing and special characters.

It also provides `\SaveVerb`/`\UseVerb` to store verbatim content for later reuse, `\DefineVerbatimEnvironment` for creating custom verbatim-like environments, and the `\VerbatimInput` command to include external files with the same options. This makes it useful for typesetting code, configuration files, and examples where exact formatting matters.

`fancyvrb` is more capable than the standard `verbatim` but less feature-rich than `listings` or `minted` for syntax highlighting. It does not colour code by language, but it is much simpler and works without external tools. It is often used for short snippets where highlighting is not needed, or as the base for other packages. It is compatible with `hyperref` and `xcolor` (for `bgcolor`). Load it in the preamble; it does not conflict with much, though it redefines some verbatim internals, so load it before packages that also patch verbatim (e.g. `comment`).

name: verbatim
desc: Provides the `verbatim` environment and `\verb` command for typesetting code or text exactly as typed, without interpreting LaTeX commands.
details:
The `verbatim` package provides the `verbatim` environment and the `\verb` command for typesetting text exactly as typed, without interpreting LaTeX commands, backslashes, or braces. It is part of the standard LaTeX distribution (the package just makes the environment available in a slightly more robust form and adds `\verbatiminput` for including files).

Use `\begin{verbatim} ... \end{verbatim}` for blocks and `\verb|...|` (or `\verb!...!` with any delimiter) for inline text. The delimiter must not appear in the content. This is ideal for showing LaTeX source, file paths, and short code snippets. The environment preserves spaces and line breaks exactly.

For anything beyond the basics, `fancyvrb` (options, line numbers, frames) or `listings`/`minted` (syntax highlighting) are better. The `verbatim` package's main advantage is that it requires no options and is always available. A common gotcha is that `\verb` cannot be used inside other commands' arguments (e.g. `\section{\verb|x|}` fails), and the `verbatim` environment cannot appear inside a macro argument. Use `\texttt{...}` with escaped characters for small inline snippets when `\verb` is not allowed.

name: textcomp
desc: Adds many text‑mode symbols (e.g., copyright, trademark, currency signs, arrows) that are not available in the basic fonts.
details:
`textcomp` provides a large set of text-mode symbols that are not available in the basic LaTeX fonts: the copyright symbol (`\textcopyright`), registered trademark (`\textregistered`), trademark (`\texttrademark`), the Euro sign (`\texteuro`), the Yen sign (`\textyen`), the degree sign (`\textdegree`), the per-mille sign (`\textperthousand`), daggers (`\textdagger`), and many more. It also gives text-mode versions of arrows and other glyphs.

The package is especially useful with the T1 font encoding and `lmodern`, where these glyphs are actually available in the font. Without `textcomp`, you might get missing-glyph warnings or have to rely on the `
\textcompwordmark` workarounds. It also provides the `\oldstylenums{...}` command for old-style figures (if the font supports them).

Many of these symbols are also available through `fontspec` with OpenType fonts, but for pdfLaTeX, `textcomp` is the standard way to get them. It should be loaded after `fontenc`. Note that with the `T1` encoding and `lmodern`, the glyphs look consistent with the rest of the document. In modern LaTeX distributions, `textcomp` is often loaded automatically by other packages, but loading it explicitly is harmless and documents that you need the extra symbols.

name: fontspec
desc: Allows you to use system fonts (OpenType, TrueType) with XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX, giving access to advanced font features.
details:
`fontspec` is the package that lets XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX use system fonts (OpenType, TrueType). You write `\setmainfont{TeX Gyre Pagella}`, `\setsansfont{...}`, and `\setmonofont{...}`, and the document uses those fonts. You can also select features like small caps (`\setmainfont[Numbers=OldStyle]{...}`) and use `\newfontfamily` for additional families. It is one of the main reasons to choose XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX over pdfLaTeX.

The package exposes OpenType features: ligatures, stylistic sets, old-style figures, swashes, and language-specific shaping. You can specify font files by name (if installed) or by path (`Path=./fonts/, Extension=.otf`). It also provides `\addfontfeatures{...}` for local changes and `\fontspec` for defining new font families. It handles fallback fonts for missing glyphs (`\newfontface`/`\fontspec` with `RawFeature`).

`fontspec` requires XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX; it does not work with pdfLaTeX. It must be loaded **before** other font-related packages (but after the document class). For maths, pair it with `unicode-math` (which sets up a Unicode maths font). A common gotcha is that the font name must be the family name, not the file name (unless you use `Path`/`Extension`). Also, fontspec does not support all legacy `fontenc` encodings — with fontspec you generally do not load `fontenc` or `inputenc`.

name: unicode-math
desc: Enables the use of OpenType math fonts (e.g., Latin Modern Math, STIX Two Math) with XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX, providing full Unicode math support.
details:
`unicode-math` brings Unicode and OpenType maths fonts to XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX. You set a maths font with `\setmathfont{Latin Modern Math}` (or `STIX Two Math`, `XITS Math`, `Libertinus Math`, etc.), and then all maths symbols are taken from that font. It replaces the traditional maths font setup and gives you access to thousands of Unicode symbols, proper OpenType maths layout, and consistent typography between text and maths.

It defines commands like `\symbf{...}` (bold maths), `\symup`, `\symit`, `\symcal`, and `\symbb`, which are the Unicode-era replacements for `\mathbf`, `\mathrm`, `\mathit`, `\mathcal`, `\mathbb`. The `\setmathfont` can be followed by `[range=...]` to use different fonts for specific Unicode blocks (e.g. a calligraphic font for script letters). It also provides `\mathup`, `\mathnormal`, and `\mathrm` compatibility.

`unicode-math` requires `fontspec` and a Unicode maths font installed on the system. It is a one-way replacement: do not mix it with `amsmath`'s font-based commands or `bm` (use `\symbf` instead of `\bm`). It also changes how some symbols are accessed, so existing documents may need adjustments (e.g. `\mathbb` becomes `\symbb` or still works). For new documents with XeLaTeX/LuaLaTeX, `unicode-math` plus a good maths font gives excellent results. It is incompatible with `mathptmx`/`newtxmath`-style packages, which are pdfLaTeX-only.

name: polyglossia
desc: A modern alternative to `babel` for XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX, offering easy language switching and font setup for many scripts.
details:
`polyglossia` is the multilingual package for XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX, designed as a modern alternative to `babel`. It handles hyphenation, language-specific typography, and font switching for scripts (Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, etc.). You load it with `\usepackage{polyglossia}`, set the main language with `\setmainlanguage{english}`, and add others with `\setotherlanguage{french}`.

It integrates with `fontspec` to switch fonts per language: `\newfontfamily\arabicfont[Script=Arabic]{Amiri}` and then `\setotherlanguage{arabic}` uses that font. This makes it much easier to typeset documents that mix scripts, because the font, hyphenation patterns, and directionality switch automatically. It also handles language-specific quotation marks and date formats when used with `csquotes`.

`polyglossia` is not compatible with `babel`; choose one. For XeLaTeX/LuaLaTeX, `polyglossia` is often the better choice for non-Latin scripts, while `babel` has better coverage for some European languages. For pdfLaTeX, `polyglossia` does not work — use `babel`. A common gotcha is that `polyglossia` must be loaded after `fontspec`, and the main language must be set before other languages. It works well with `unicode-math` and `csquotes` for fully multilingual documents.

name: beamer
desc: A document class for producing slides and presentations in PDF, with themes, overlays, and navigation.
details:
`beamer` is the dominant LaTeX class for presentations. Unlike most packages, it is a **document class**: `\documentclass{beamer}`. It provides a `frame` environment for slides, themes (`\usetheme{Madrid}`), colour themes, and navigation bars. It supports overlays (`\pause`, `\onslide`, `\only`, `\uncover`) so content appears incrementally, which is a key feature for teaching and talks.

A typical slide is `\begin{frame}{Title} content \end{frame}`. Content is typeset in a 4:3 or 16:9 aspect ratio (set with the class option `aspectratio=169`). Beamer has `block` environments (`block`, `alertblock`, `exampleblock`) for emphasised content, `columns` for multi-column layouts, and `\againframe` to repeat a slide. The `\titlepage` and `\maketitle` setup is standard. It also has a `handout` mode (`\documentclass[handout]{beamer}`) that removes overlays for printing.

Beamer is powerful but has a learning curve: its default themes look dated, and good customisation requires some effort. Modern themes like `metropolis` give a cleaner look. Beamer's `\pause` and overlays can slow compilation for large decks; consider `\usepackage{beamerarticle}` for a printable article version. Beamer is based on `pgf`/`tikz`, so `tikz` pictures work natively. It plays well with `biblatex` (for references) and `listings`/`minted` (for code), but `enumitem` is not compatible — use beamer's own list options.

name: pdfpages
desc: Allows you to insert pages from external PDF files (e.g., `\includepdf{file.pdf}`) and to combine multiple PDFs into one document.
details:
`pdfpages` includes pages from external PDF files into your document. The main command is `\includepdf[pages=-]{file.pdf}`, which inserts the entire PDF (`pages=-`) or selected pages (`pages=1,3,5-7`). Options include `nup` (to place multiple pages per sheet, e.g. `nup=2x2`), `landscape`, `frame`, `scale`, `offset`, and `pagecommand` (to add content like a header to each page).

This is useful for combining separate PDFs (e.g. a cover page, several articles, and an appendix) into one document, or for creating booklets and handouts. `\includepdf` works with any PDF, regardless of how it was produced, so it is a way to embed a document generated by another tool. It also provides the `\includepdfmerge` command for merging several files in one go.

`pdfpages` requires pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX, or LuaLaTeX (it cannot be used with plain DVI). It works at the page level, so the included pages keep their original size and orientation (use `fitpaper`/`landscape` to adjust). It is often used with `nup` to create 2-up or 4-up handouts. Note that `\includepdf` inserts pages as full-page content and does not interact with the surrounding text layout; for partial-page inclusion, use `\includegraphics` with `page=...` from `graphicx` instead. It is also the standard tool for creating a "PDF of PDFs" without external tools.

name: standalone
desc: Enables you to compile individual figures or tables as standalone PDFs and then include them in a main document, speeding up compilation.

name: import
desc: Provides `\import` and `\subimport` to include files from different folders, with correct handling of relative paths.
details:
LaTeX resolves `\input{chapters/intro.tex}` relative to the *main* file's directory, and the same is true for `\includegraphics`. That breaks as soon as `chapters/intro.tex` itself says `\input{sec/part1}` — LaTeX will look for `sec/part1.tex` next to the main file, not next to `intro.tex`. The `import` package fixes exactly this by temporarily prepending the imported file's directory to `\input@path`, the list LaTeX searches.

```latex
% main.tex
\usepackage{import}
\import{chapters/}{intro.tex}

% chapters/intro.tex
\subimport{sections/}{part1.tex}   % finds chapters/sections/part1.tex
```

`\subimport` *appends* to the current search path, so nested imports accumulate directories; `\import` *resets* it to the main directory, which is what you want when a chapter should be self-contained. The `\inputfrom`, `\includefrom` and starred variants (`\import*`) give the same behaviour for `\include` and for cases where you do not want the path to be reset. Because `\input@path` is also consulted by `graphicx`'s file search, figures inside an imported file are usually found without extra `\graphicspath` entries.

Two caveats. `import` changes the search path globally for the duration of the `\import`, so a file that relies on being found next to the *main* document may stop working — use absolute paths or `\graphicspath` to be safe. And `import` is not a project-management tool: for a book-length project, `subfiles` or a build script (e.g. `latexmk` with `\input` plus `\graphicspath`) is often the cleaner solution.

name: subfiles
desc: Allows you to split a large document into sub‑files that can be compiled independently while sharing a common preamble.

name: xr
desc: Lets you reference labels in external LaTeX documents (e.g., `\externaldocument{file}`) so that `\ref` works across files.
details:
`xr` makes `\ref` work across documents by reading another document's `.aux` file. You declare the external document in the preamble with an optional prefix, and every label defined in that document becomes available under `prefix-name`.

```latex
\usepackage{xr}
\externaldocument[ch1-]{chapter1}   % reads chapter1.aux
...
See Section~\ref{ch1-methods}.
```

With `hyperref` loaded, use `xr-hyper` instead of `xr` (it is a drop-in replacement) so that the resulting references are real hyperlinks pointing into the other PDF. The prefix is not cosmetic: without it, two documents that both define `sec:intro` will silently collide, with the last-loaded definition winning. Because the labels come from the `.aux` file, the external document must be compiled *before* the referencing one, and every time the external numbering changes you have to recompile in the right order — a `latexmk` setup with explicit dependencies handles this well.

`xr` supports `\ref` and `\pageref`; newer versions also handle `\nameref` and `\autoref`-style prefixes. It does not copy the external document's *counters* into your document, so if both use different section numbering schemes the printed numbers may look inconsistent. A common and tidy alternative is to build one master document and use `subfiles`, which avoids cross-document references altogether.

name: bookmark
desc: Provides finer control over PDF bookmarks (e.g., adding bookmarks for sections that are not numbered) when used together with `hyperref`.
details:
`hyperref` creates PDF bookmarks automatically for `\section`, `\chapter` and friends, but it has nothing to offer for `\section*{Acknowledgements}`, for a title page, or for a “Part I” divider that you typeset by hand. The `bookmark` package fills that gap with `\bookmark`, which adds a single entry to the PDF outline without touching the document body.

```latex
\usepackage{bookmark}   % after hyperref
...
\bookmark[level=1,dest=sec:intro]{1  Introduction}
\bookmark[level=0]{Front matter}
```

The key–value interface understands `level`, `dest`, `rellevel`, `color`, `italic`, `bold` and `named`, plus `startatroot` in `\bookmarksetup` to return to the top level after a `\part`. `\currentpdfbookmark`, `\subpdfbookmark` and `\belowpdfbookmark` are shorthands for the three common placements. `\bookmarkAtEnd` defers the insertion so it happens after the whole document — handy for a “References” entry when the bibliography is generated by an external tool.

Two rules: load it *after* `hyperref` (it patches hyperref internals), and if the destination of a bookmark is not defined yet, the entry will silently point nowhere — check the resulting PDF outline rather than the log. The `draft` option disables all bookmark creation, which is useful for debugging hyperref interactions.

name: nameref
desc: Extends `hyperref` to allow referencing the name of a section (e.g., `\nameref{sec:intro}`) rather than just its number.
details:
`\nameref{sec:method}` prints the *title* of the referenced section rather than its number — “see Section 3.2 (Numerical results)” becomes possible without hard-coding the words. It also produces a hyperlink to the section when `hyperref` is active. `\Nameref` capitalises the first letter, and the starred form `\nameref*` drops the link.

```latex
As discussed in \nameref{sec:methods}, ...
```

`hyperref` loads `nameref` automatically, so the command is available in any document that uses hyperref; loading `\usepackage{nameref}` explicitly is only needed to set options, of which `nameinlink` (make the title itself a link) is the useful one. The most common complaint is that `\nameref` inside a `\section` title, a caption, or a running header causes errors — the title is being read while the label it points to is still undefined, and `nameref`'s internal expansion cannot handle that. The standard fix is `\texorpdfstring` or `\protect`.

It is also worth knowing that `\nameref` uses the *last* value written to the `.aux` file, so a label placed before its title (e.g. on the first line of a section) yields an empty result on the first run and the correct one on the second. This is normal, not a bug — but it does mean `\nameref` output should not be relied on in a one-pass build.

name: doi
desc: Provides commands to format Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) as clickable links, often used in bibliographies.
details:
`doi` is a tiny package whose entire job is to typeset a Digital Object Identifier as a clickable link with consistent formatting. `\doi{10.1000/xyz123}` produces “doi:10.1000/xyz123”, where the identifier is an `\href` to `https://doi.org/...`. The `\doitext` macro can be redefined if you prefer “DOI” or no label at all.

```latex
\usepackage{doi}
...
\doi{10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.061102}
```

It plays well with `hyperref` (it uses `\href` internally when available and degrades to plain text otherwise) and is mostly used inside bibliography entries or a `note` field, since `natbib` and `biblatex` styles already emit DOIs from the `.bib` file. If your style produces a bare `doi:` prefix and you want the link to be clickable, loading `doi` and redefining `\doitext` is the least invasive fix.

Note that, unlike `biblatex`'s `doi` field, this package does not validate the identifier or strip a `https://doi.org/` prefix for you — pass the bare `10.xxxx/...` form.

name: orcidlink
desc: Adds a command (`\orcidlink{...}`) to include a clickable ORCID icon and link in documents.
details:
`\orcidlink{0000-0002-1825-0097}` typesets the green ORCID iD icon followed by a hyperlink to the author's ORCID profile. It is designed for the author block of a paper, where a list of names and affiliations benefits from one-click access to each researcher's record.

```latex
\usepackage{orcidlink}
\author{Ada Lovelace\,\orcidlink{0000-0002-1825-0097}}
```

The package requires `hyperref` (it builds the link with `\href`) and ships the icon as a vector PDF, so it scales cleanly and prints well in both colour and greyscale. Because the icon is included with `\includegraphics`, it also needs `graphicx` — which `hyperref` pulls in anyway.

For a publication you will often want the ORCID to appear only in the PDF and not in the metadata; wrap it in `\texorpdfstring{\orcidlink{...}}{}` when it sits inside a `\section` or a caption. The `academicons` package offers `\aiOrcid` as a font-based alternative if you would rather keep everything as glyphs.

name: academicons
desc: Provides a set of icons for academic services (e.g., Google Scholar, ResearchGate, ORCID) that can be used in documents.

name: fontawesome5
desc: Gives access to the Font Awesome 5 icon set, allowing you to insert icons (e.g., `\faIcon{github}`) in your document.
details:
`fontawesome5` gives LaTeX access to the Font Awesome 5 icon set — thousands of glyphs for brands, UI elements, arrows and symbols. The canonical interface is `\faIcon{name}` (e.g. `\faIcon{github}`, `\faIcon{envelope}`), and the package also defines direct shortcuts such as `\faGithub` and `\faCoffee` for the most common icons.

```latex
\usepackage{fontawesome5}
...
\href{https://github.com/you}{\faIcon{github}}~you
```

Useful options are `fixedwidth` (all icons get the same width, which keeps lists and table columns aligned) and `pro` for the paid icon set; icons are text-mode glyphs, so they follow the surrounding font size and colour and can be used inside `\href`, `\section`, item labels or `\begin{itemize}[label=\faIcon{check}]`.

Because glyph names change between Font Awesome versions, an icon that worked with `fontawesome` (v4) may need renaming for `fontawesome5`; the package documentation has a mapping table. And, as with any icon font, avoid using an icon as the *only* marker of meaning — screen readers and greyscale printers will lose it.

name: marvosym
desc: Provides a collection of symbols such as Euro, smileys, checkmarks, and information signs.
details:
`marvosym` is an old but still handy symbol font covering everyday pictograms: smileys (`\Smiley`, `\Frownie`, `\Neutral`), check marks (`\Checkmark`, `\Cross`), communication icons (`\Telefon`, `\Mobilefone`, `\Letter`, `\Email`, `\Info`), currencies (`\EUR`, `\Euro`) and a set of astronomical and zodiac symbols.

```latex
\usepackage{marvosym}
...
\EUR{10} \quad \Telefon{} +49 30 1234
```

`\EUR{...}` is the reason many people still load the package: it typesets the euro sign with the correct amount spacing. Note that `\EUR` takes an argument while `\Euro` is the bare symbol.

The package is text-mode oriented and mixes well with `pifont` and `wasysym`, but its glyph names are occasionally redefined by other packages and the fonts have a distinctly 1990s look. It is also worth knowing that `marvosym` does not provide scalable icons — for a modern document `fontawesome5` will usually look better; `marvosym` remains useful where a symbol must exist in Type1 form for a journal's PDF workflow.

name: pifont
desc: Loads the Zapf Dingbats font and provides commands to access its symbols (e.g., `\ding{43}` for a checkmark).
details:
`pifont` is the standard way to reach the Zapf Dingbats glyphs. The command `\ding{n}` prints glyph number *n* of the font (the numbering is documented in the package manual), and the generic `\Pisymbol{pzd}{n}` does the same thing through a mechanism that can also address other PostScript symbol fonts.

```latex
\usepackage{pifont}
\ding{51}~\ding{55}~\ding{43}
```

The package also provides the `dinglist` and `dingautolist` environments for itemised lists whose bullets are dingbats, and `\dingfill`/`\dingline` for decorative rules — the latter two are genuinely useful for certificates and posters. In `beamer`, `\ding{...}` is a common source of bullet symbols because it needs no TikZ.

The most frequent use in practice is `\ding{51}` and `\ding{55}` as check/cross marks in tables. Remember that these are ordinary glyphs and inherit `\color` normally; and if a journal rejects bitmap fonts, check that the `pzd` font is embedded (it usually is).

name: wasysym
desc: Offers a wide range of extra symbols (astronomical, biological, chemical, etc.) for text and math mode.
details:
`wasysym` — “WAsy SYmbols” — adds a broad set of text- and math-mode symbols that the base fonts lack: smileys (`\smiley`, `\frownie`), boxes (`\Square`, `\CheckedBox`, `\XBox`), gender signs (`\Female`, `\Male`), phones and letters, astronomy (`\Sun`, `\Moon`), and a collection of electrical and musical symbols.

```latex
\usepackage[nointegrals]{wasysym}
...
\CheckedBox{} done \quad \Square{} pending \quad \Phone{} 555-0100
```

The package is famous for two things. The first is `nointegrals`, an option that stops wasysym from redefining the `\int` family — without it, integral signs change shape, which is not what you want in a maths paper. The second is a set of name clashes with `amssymb` (`\Box`, `\Diamond`, `\Join`, `\leadsto`, `\lhd`, `\unlhd`, `\sqsubset`, `\sqsupset` …), because both packages want to own the same names. Load `amssymb` *first* and wasysym after, or better, load wasysym with `nointegrals` and be explicit about which definition you want.

Because the glyphs come from a Type1 font with limited coverage, wasysym should be treated as a convenience rather than a complete icon set; for anything decorative, `fontawesome5` or a TikZ drawing will scale better.

name: amsfonts
desc: Provides the AMS fonts (msam, msbm) and the commands `\mathfrak` and `\mathbb`. `amssymb` loads `amsfonts` automatically.
details:
`amsfonts` is the original American Mathematical Society font package. It supplies two fonts, `msam` and `msbm`, and with them the commands `\mathbb` (blackboard bold, for `\mathbb{R}`, `\mathbb{N}`, `\mathbb{Z}`) and `\mathfrak` (Fraktur, for Lie algebras and ideals).

```latex
\usepackage{amsfonts}
\mathbb{R}^n, \quad \mathfrak{g} \cong \mathfrak{sl}_2
```

In practice you rarely load it directly: `amssymb` loads `amsfonts` for you, and `amssymb` also provides the rest of the AMS symbol fonts. Loading `amsfonts` explicitly is only necessary if you want `\mathbb`/`\mathfrak` without the (large) symbol set, or if you are debugging an “undefined control sequence” error and want to know which package was supposed to provide the command.

Two limitations are worth remembering. `\mathbb` in msbm covers *uppercase letters only* — `\mathbb{1}` and `\mathbb{r}` produce nothing, which is why the `bbm` and `dsfont` packages exist. And `\mathfrak` is not the same as `\mathcal`; if a paper uses script letters for function spaces, that is `mathrsfs`.

name: latexsym
desc: Provides additional symbols (e.g., `\Box`, `\Diamond`) that were part of the original LaTeX symbol font but are not available by default.
details:
`latexsym` loads the `lasy` font, which contains the symbols that were promised in the original LaTeX manual but never made it into the default set: `\Box`, `\Diamond`, `\mho`, `\Join`, `\leadsto`, `\sqsubset`, `\sqsupset`, `\lhd`, `\rhd`, `\unlhd`, `\unrhd` and a few arrow-like glyphs.

```latex
\usepackage{latexsym}
A \sqsubset B \quad \Box \Diamond
```

The package exists mainly for backwards compatibility: `amssymb` provides every one of these symbols in a better-designed form, so in a modern document you should load `amssymb` and forget about `latexsym`. Loading both is actively a bad idea — the names collide and the last one loaded wins, giving you symbols of inconsistent weight in the same formula.

Keep it in mind only when you are working with a very old template, or when a journal's class file loads it for you and you need to understand why `\Box` looks different from the one in your own notes.

name: stmaryrd
desc: Adds symbols commonly used in theoretical computer science (e.g., `\llbracket`, `\rrbracket`, `\bigsqcap`).
details:
`stmaryrd` (St Mary Road) is the symbol package for theoretical computer science and semantics: semantic brackets `\llbracket`/`\rrbracket`, `\llparenthesis`/`\rrparenthesis`, the lattice operators `\bigsqcap` and `\bigsqcup`, `\fatsemi`, `\Yup`, `\varcurlyvee`, and a large family of short arrows such as `\shortrightarrow`.

```latex
\usepackage{stmaryrd}
\llbracket e \rrbracket \quad \bigsqcap_{i} S_i
```

All of these are maths-mode only and are designed to sit alongside `amsmath`/`amssymb`, which should be loaded first. The main limitation is that the bracket delimiters come in a single size: `\left\llbracket` and `\right\rrbracket` will not grow with a tall formula. For tall semantics, the usual workaround is to declare a paired delimiter with `mathtools` (`\DeclarePairedDelimiter{\sem}{\llbracket}{\rrbracket}`) and pass `\big`/`\Big` sizes explicitly.

One more thing to know: `stmaryrd` predates Unicode math and uses its own font encoding, so the glyphs will not survive a copy-paste out of the PDF, and they may look slightly lighter than Computer Modern. That is cosmetic, but it matters if you are matching a publisher's house style.

name: mathrsfs
desc: Provides the `\mathscr` command for a calligraphic script font in math mode, often used for sets and spaces.
details:
`mathrsfs` provides one command, `\mathscr`, and one font: the Ralph Smith Formal Script, a highly slanted calligraphic face. It is traditionally used for function spaces and sigma-algebras — `\mathscr{F}`, `\mathscr{L}`, `\mathscr{H}` — and for anything where `\mathcal` looks too upright.

```latex
\usepackage{mathrsfs}
\mathscr{L}^2(\mathbb{R}) \subset \mathscr{S}'
```

The font contains *uppercase letters only*; `\mathscr{a}` produces nothing useful, so for script lowercase you need a different font (e.g. `\mathcal` or a `unicode-math` script alphabet). It does not modify `\mathcal`, so you can use both in the same document, though mixing the two script styles in one formula is usually a mistake.

Because the glyphs are fairly extreme in slope, they read poorly in subscripts and superscripts; a common alternative is to load `unicode-math` and pick a script font that suits your text font. `mathrsfs` remains the pragmatic choice for pdfLaTeX users who just need `\mathscr{F}`.

name: bbm
desc: Offers an alternative blackboard bold font (`\mathbbm`) with better spacing than the standard `\mathbb`.
details:
`bbm` provides a family of blackboard-bold (double-struck) fonts with far better coverage than `amsfonts`: lowercase letters, digits, and sans-serif and typewriter variants via `\mathbbmss` and `\mathbbmtt`. The killer feature is `\mathbbm{1}`, the indicator function — a glyph that simply does not exist in `\mathbb`.

```latex
\usepackage{bbm}
\mathbbm{1}_{A} \quad \mathbbmss{R} \quad \mathbbmtt{x}
```

`\mathbbm` covers upper- and lowercase Latin letters and digits; `\mathbbmss` and `\mathbbmtt` are the sans-serif and monospaced equivalents, which are useful for distinguishing, say, a random variable from its realisation. The fonts are part of a standard TeX Live installation, so no extra setup is needed.

Style note: `\mathbbm{1}` and `\mathds{1}` (from `dsfont`) are the two standard ways to write an indicator; pick one and be consistent, because the glyphs differ subtly in weight and width. `bbm` is the older of the two and its glyphs are slightly bolder.

name: dsfont
desc: Provides the `\mathds` command for double‑struck (blackboard bold) letters, with a slightly different style than `amsfonts`.
details:
`dsfont` provides `\mathds`, a double-struck alphabet whose most popular glyph is `\mathds{1}` for the indicator function. It competes directly with `bbm`; the differences are stylistic — `dsfont`'s digits are a little lighter and its uppercase letters are closer to Computer Modern in width.

```latex
\usepackage{dsfont}
\mathds{1}_{x > 0} \qquad \mathds{R}^d
```

The package offers `sans` and `light` options to select alternative font weights, which is handy if you are matching a document that uses a sans-serif maths font. As with `bbm`, coverage is limited to letters and digits; there is no `\mathds{\alpha}`.

A practical warning: some journals' class files already load a double-struck font, and adding another font package on top can silently change the appearance of formulas elsewhere in the document. After adding it, re-read a few pages that use `\mathbb` or `\mathds` to make sure nothing shifted.

name: upgreek
desc: Allows Greek letters to be typeset upright (e.g., `\upalpha`) instead of the default italic, which is common in some physics and engineering contexts.
details:
By default LaTeX sets Greek letters in maths as italics, which is correct for variables but wrong when a Greek letter is a *unit* or a *constant name*. `upgreek` provides upright versions of all the lowercase and uppercase Greek letters: `\upalpha`, `\upbeta`, … `\upOmega`.

```latex
\usepackage[Euler]{upgreek}
5\,\upmu\mathrm{m} \quad \uppi \approx 3.14159
```

The package has to borrow glyphs from some other font, and the option selects which: `Euler` (the default), `Symbol`, `Symbolsmallscale` and `Adobe`. The choice affects both the shape and whether lowercase letters are available, so check the output — `\upmu` in particular is frequently used for micrometres and must match the surrounding text font.

If you are using `unicode-math` with XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX, do not load `upgreek`: `unicode-math` already provides `\upalpha` and friends, and the two packages will fight over the command names. Similarly, if you use `siunitx` for units you rarely need `upgreek` at all, because siunitx handles the upright Greek in unit macros.

name: textgreek
desc: Provides commands to typeset Greek letters in text mode (e.g., `\textalpha`) without switching to math mode.
details:
`textgreek` provides Greek letters in *text* mode — `\textalpha`, `\textbeta`, `\textpi`, `\textmu` — which is what you want when a Greek letter is part of a word, an abbreviation or a unit name rather than a mathematical variable.

```latex
\usepackage[LGR,T1]{fontenc}
\usepackage{textgreek}
\textmu m \quad \textOmega
```

With pdfLaTeX you need a font that has the LGR encoding, typically by loading `\usepackage[LGR,T1]{fontenc}` (and a font family that supports it). With XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX you instead need `fontspec` and a system font containing Greek; `textgreek` will then use whatever text font is current. The package has a few font-selection options (e.g. `artemisia`, `euripides`, `stix`) for choosing which Greek face to use in the pdfLaTeX case.

The classic use is `\textmu` for the “micro” prefix, since `\mu` is an italic maths variable and looks wrong in “µm”. Be aware that the input encoding matters: with `inputenc` and UTF-8 you can also type the Greek characters directly, and `textgreek` mainly earns its keep in older or mixed setups.

name: units
desc: An older package for typesetting units (e.g., `\unit{9.81}{\metre\per\second\squared}`). Most new documents should use `siunitx` instead.
